1.t: Abu Nour and the Lost Boats
1.tz: On a night when the sea is black, a light turns on the Old Lighthouse. Who guides the lost boats home?

secs.h: Chapter One: The Night the Sea Turned Black [خيال]
b: Listen, my friend. One night, when the sea was black as ink and the waves were fighting with the quay, a little boy named Salem was walking alone along the Port Said Corniche. Salem was the son of a fisherman, one of those who sail out into Lake Manzala, and his father had not come back from fishing since the morning.
The wind buzzed in his ears, the water slapped the stones, and the street lights trembled. Salem walked and looked toward the sea, and said to himself: Dear God, bring my father back safe.

Suddenly, far away, he saw something shine. Not a star, and not a fisherman's lamp. A great light, turning and turning, wiping away the whole darkness the way a mother strokes her child's head. Salem raised his eyes and found the Old Lighthouse standing in its place, tall and thin, with the light turning above it.
And Salem said to himself: Strange. People say this lighthouse went dark a long time ago.

secs.h: Chapter Two: The Lighthouse As It Really Is [حقيقة]
b: Before we go on, let me tell you the truth behind this place. The Old Lighthouse in Port Said was built around 1869, the same year the Suez Canal opened to navigation. It was built by the French, so that boats and ships could reach the canal entrance safely at night. It is about 56 meters tall and octagonal, meaning it has eight sides. Most importantly, it is one of the first buildings in the world made of reinforced concrete, at a time when people were still building with stone.

The lighthouse kept lighting the way for ships for many years, until it stopped working around 1997, when a new lighthouse was built. So the light that used to turn on top of it really did go out decades ago. That is what made Salem wonder.
(Sources: 1, 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)

Salem came closer to the lighthouse, his feet stumbling in the sand. The closer he got, the warmer the light became, not an electric light but a light like a candle in his grandmother's house. When he reached the very foot of the lighthouse, he heard a voice laughing from above, a relaxed laugh.
"Hey kid, scared?"
Salem looked up and found a small man in a white galabiya and a yellow turban, his face glowing on its own. He sat on the edge of the lighthouse balcony with his legs dangling.
"I am Abu Nour," said the man. "A good ifrit. Not one of those that scare people, no. I am one of those who hold the light."
Salem swallowed: "And why are you holding the light, uncle?"

"For the boats, my son. I have lived here since the day the lighthouse was built. People forgot the lighthouse, but the sea still remembers. Every night there is a lost boat, a fisherman or a sailor, I see him from above and I turn the light on him until he finds his way."

secs.h: Chapter Four: The Old Story of Abu Nour [خيال]
b: Abu Nour sat down, stretched out his legs and said: "Would you like me to tell you how I became Abu Nour?"
Salem nodded.

"Long ago, before this city was a city, there was only sand, sea and a lake. People came from everywhere to dig the canal. People from Upper Egypt, people from Nubia, people from abroad. They worked with their hands in the sun. At night they sat around the fire and sang."

[حقيقة] The real story: Port Said was founded in 1859 with the start of the canal digging, and in the early days the work was done by the hands of many laborers. They say the first song they sang was "Ya Haly", and later came the art of the simsimiyya and the Damma that the city became famous for. (Sources 4 and 5.)

[خيال] "One of the workers was named Nour," Abu Nour went on. "He had a voice that could make stone weep. One night his friend got lost in the fog on his way back from work, and Nour kept singing and singing until his friend heard his voice and found his way. Since then people say: whoever's voice brings back the lost deserves to have his name live on."
"And when Nour died," Abu Nour lowered his voice, "his light did not go away. It stayed in the lighthouse. I became his friend and the keeper of his light. That is why my name is Abu Nour."

secs.h: Chapter Five: Why Did the Light Come On Tonight? [خيال]
b: Salem asked: "And today? I have not seen a lit lighthouse since the day I was born."

Abu Nour smiled: "Tonight there is a lost boat. A small boat in the middle of the lake, the fog coming down on it, and the fisherman in it cannot find his way. And my light alone is not enough. I need someone down there to remember."
"Remember what?"

"Remember the stories, Salem. This lighthouse does not run on electricity. It runs on stories. Every time someone tells a story about Port Said, the light grows. When people forgot, the light faded. And you came tonight remembering your father, so the light came back."
Salem felt his heart pounding. His father was on that boat?
"Yes," said Abu Nour, as if he had heard. "Your father's boat is the lost one. But don't worry. We will bring him back together. But first, there is a condition."
"I don't let anyone go up and touch the light without proving they understand Port Said," said Abu Nour. "I will ask you a riddle. If you answer right, the light will reach your father."
Salem stood up straight and said: "Ask."
And in a voice that rang like a bell, Abu Nour said:
Salem thought. He looked around, looked at the sea, looked up. And suddenly he smiled.
(The answer: the lighthouse. In the game: the player types or picks the answer from 3 choices: the lighthouse, the boat, the port.)
"The lighthouse!" said Salem in a loud voice.
Abu Nour laughed a laugh that shook the balcony. "Bravo, son of a good man. You do understand."

Abu Nour stretched out his hand, and the lighthouse beam made one big turn and swept the whole lake all the way to Manzala. And Salem saw with his own eyes, very far away, a small candle moving, his father's boat.
"Do you see it?" asked Abu Nour.
"I see it!"
"Tell him to follow the light."
And Salem shouted from below with all his strength: "Dad! Follow the light!"
And from far away, in the middle of the fog, he heard his father's voice, weak but clear: "Salem? Is that you, Salem?"

And the light kept turning and turning, and the boat came closer. For a whole hour Salem and Abu Nour took turns talking. Abu Nour told stories about the boats that passed here long ago, big ships from all over the world, people wearing tarbooshes and people wearing the "balma", the hat worn by the Bumboutis, the people who went out in small boats to sell goods to passing ships.

[حقيقة] The Bumboutis really were people of Port Said who worked in sea trade with ships passing through the canal, and their name comes from the English word "boatman", meaning a man of the boat, which people twisted into "bambouti". Their well-known dress included a hat called the "balma". (Source 6.)
[خيال] And with every story the light grew stronger, and the boat came nearer.

secs.h: Chapter Seven (continued): The Bambouti Who Sold to the Ifrit [خيال]
b: To make the time pass and the boat come closer, Abu Nour told Salem a funny story.

"Long ago," said Abu Nour, swinging his legs, "there was a Bambouti named Uncle Shehta, whose tongue was longer than the canal itself. He used to go out in his little boat to the ships and sell the sailors everything: watches, tassels, galabiyas, and pharaoh statues stamped Made in Port Said. One night he saw a strange ship standing at the entrance, without a single light on it."
"A ghost ship?" asked Salem, his eyes wide.

"Wait. Uncle Shehta climbed aboard saying: Welcome, boss, I have the best goods in the world for you! And he found in front of him a tall captain with a pale face, looking at him without a word. Uncle Shehta did not flinch. He kept talking: this is a Swiss watch, this one is genuine, this has a one year warranty. And the captain stayed silent. When he got tired of talking he said: Okay, how much will you take for it, boss, name a number!"
Salem laughed: "And then?"

"The captain opened his mouth and said in a voice coming from under the earth: I have been dead for three hundred years, uncle. What would I do with a watch? And Uncle Shehta answered without blinking: Maybe you need to know how much time you have left! And the captain laughed until he vanished, and left a bag of gold in his hand. Since then they say the Bumboutis sell even to ifrits."
And Abu Nour laughed until the light on top of the lighthouse shook. "That is why, Salem, in Port Said even fear turns into a joke."
And over the sound of that laughter, from very far away, came the sound of a simsimiyya. A tune both sad and happy at the same time, the way the tune is in this city.
[حقيقة] The simsimiyya really is a folk instrument tied to the canal cities, and Port Said especially, and they also call it "the Nadaha" because its sound pulls people toward it. (Source 7.)
[خيال] "That is the voice of an old woman singing to her son out at sea," said Abu Nour. "She sings every night. And whoever sings for someone brings them safety."
At last the boat reached the quay. Salem's father stepped off, soaked from head to foot, but alive and well. Salem ran to him and they hugged.
"How did you find the way?" asked the father.
"There was a light," said Salem, "the lighthouse light."
The father looked at the lighthouse and said: "But that lighthouse has been off for years, my son."
Salem looked up. Abu Nour was standing at the balcony, waving his hand, and then the light began to fade until it disappeared.
"No," said Salem with a smile. "It is not off. It is just waiting."

secs.h: Chapter Nine: Abu Nour's Last Words [خيال]
b: And before he vanished completely, Salem heard Abu Nour's voice reaching him on the wind:

"Tell the stories, Salem. Tell about the lighthouse, and about Port Said, and about the people who dug the canal, and about the Bumboutis, and about the simsimiyya. Every story you tell lights up a boat somewhere. And if people forget, the lighthouse will stay silent. But if you keep telling, it will keep turning."
And since then, my friend, when someone walks in Port Said at night and looks at the lighthouse and remembers a story, they say the light trembles a little, a tiny bit, like a wink.

secs.h: Chapter Ten: The Point of the Story
b: So what does this story mean? Fact and fiction:

[حقيقة] The Old Lighthouse really exists. The French built it around 1869 for the opening of the Suez Canal, it is 56 meters tall, made of reinforced concrete, and it stopped working around 1997. Port Said was founded in 1859 with the digging of the canal, the simsimiyya and the Damma are part of its heritage, and the Bumboutis were real people who worked with the ships passing through.
[خيال] Abu Nour, Salem, the worker Nour, the lost boat, and the riddle: all of this is our own invention, to tell the truth in a way people will love.
Your reward: the "Abu Nour" card (Rare, No. 001), and you can share it with your friends on WhatsApp.

2.t: The Ifrit Apartment: The Wall That Flew
2.p: Al-Zohour District, Amr Ibn Al-Aas Area · Port Said
2.tz: An apartment in Al-Zohour, and people say its wall moves. What is behind the story?

secs.h: Chapter One: The Sound at Dawn [حقيقة]
b: This is one of the most famous folk stories in Port Said, told for more than twenty years. It says that in 1999, at about five thirty in the morning, a powerful explosion rang out in Al-Zohour district, in an area called Amr Ibn Al-Aas. People woke up terrified and ran out onto their balconies to see what had happened.

And what they saw, according to the version that circulates, was strange. One particular apartment's wall had disappeared, as if cut with a ruler. Not ruin and broken bricks like any collapse. A wall that left its place empty, while the rest of the apartment, the doors and the belongings, looked untouched, unlike what people expected. And to this day no official body has announced an explanation of what happened, according to the sources we read.
And that is where the story began. And the rest, my friend, is people's talk.

secs.h: Chapter Two: What Was Said in the Coffeehouses [حقيقة]
b: When people found no explanation, they made their own. The most famous one, according to the press, was that the owner of the apartment had been reading a book called "Shams al-Maarif", a famous book in folk tradition said to contain spells for summoning jinn. The story says he succeeded in summoning them but could not send them away, so he locked them in the bathroom. And from here came the sentence that became the mark of the story: "The jinn took the walls and flew."

There is no documented evidence for this, of course, and the sources themselves say so. But the story grew. People began coming from everywhere to watch. The area turned into a gathering place. Tea sellers, snack sellers and chair renters appeared, and "going to the ifrit apartment" became an outing, like saying going to the Corniche. It was said people waited for an ifrit to peek out of the apartment.
This is the truth behind the story: a strange event really happened, a folk explanation was told, and a whole city decided to turn it into an evening out.
(Sources 1, 2, 3 and 4 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: What Was Never Told [خيال]
b: Now I will tell you the story from the other side. The side nobody told.

In the building where the wall was said to have flown, there was a girl named Laila, nine years old, living on the third floor. Laila woke up every day before dawn, not for prayer and not for school, but because she was hearing something. Something like a whisper, coming from the bathroom.
The first time she heard it, she thought it was the pipes. The second time, she thought it was the wind. But on the third night she heard the whisper say her name.
"Laila... Laila..."
Laila got out of bed slowly, tiptoed over, and leaned her ear against the bathroom door. And the whisper said, in a thin voice like a child's: "We are bored, Laila. We are tired of the dark."

Laila opened the door with a trembling hand. There was nothing there. But the mirror above the sink was full of steam, though the water was not running. And on the steam, as if someone had written with a finger: "Open the window."

She opened the window. The blue light of dawn came in, and in that light she saw them. Three tiny ifrits, the size of her fingers, sitting on the edge of the sink. One wore a red cap and looked mischievous, one was old with a white mustache, and a small girl wore a dress made of newspaper.
"Aren't you afraid?" asked the little ifrit girl in the newspaper dress.
"No," said Laila, "but I am surprised. Who are you?"

"We are the ones who got locked in here," answered the old ifrit, his voice hoarse. "A man who read from a big book brought us, and said he would make us work for him. But the one who told us to work did not know how to tell us to leave. And we stayed here."

The ifrits told Laila everything. That the man in the apartment next to theirs, the one people call the owner of the story, was a kind but curious man. He found an old book in the book market and read from it out loud without understanding. Without meaning to, he opened a narrow door between our world and theirs, and the little ifrits came through it and fell into the bathroom.
"And we cannot get out on our own," said the ifrit in the red cap. "This door only opens from inside if someone from your side says the right word."
"The right word? What is it?"
"We don't know," said the old one. "But we know it is not in the book. The book opens the door. But what closes it is a simple word, the kind people say to each other every day."
Laila thought. Then she said: "Well, I can try words. But don't laugh at me if I get it wrong."
Laila sat on the edge of the bathtub with the three ifrits in front of her, and suddenly they started arguing with each other in low voices so nobody would hear.
"I told you from the beginning not to touch the book!" said the one in the red cap.
"Me? You are the one who said: come on, let's see what the man is doing!" answered the ifrit girl in newspaper as she straightened her dress.
"Enough, kids," said the old one, smoothing his mustache, "we have been here two hours and Laila is waiting."
"Two hours?" Laila laughed. "You have been here for years!"
"Years?" The old one looked at the two little ones. "It seems we forgot to count."

And they kept arguing about who was to blame, and about who should have known how to get back, and about who ate the last newspaper page in the bathroom. And Laila sat laughing until her tears came. And she told herself: these are the loveliest ifrits in the world, they neither scare nor hurt anyone, they just fight like my siblings.
"So what do you eat here?" she asked.
"Newspaper," said the ifrit girl proudly. "But it has gotten boring. Old news tastes bad."

And outside the bathroom, dawn was approaching, and the whole building was still asleep. Nobody knew that on the third floor three ifrits and a little girl were discovering the secret of the door. And far off, the morning newspaper seller was spreading his goods on the pavement, telling himself this would be an ordinary day. He did not know it would become the most famous day in the neighborhood, and that he would sell tea to a thousand people on that same pavement before noon.

Laila tried. She said: "Good morning." Nothing happened. She said: "In the name of God." The ifrits shivered, but the door did not move. She said: "Open sesame." The tiniest ifrit girl laughed and said: "That is another story, sweetheart."
And after trying ten words, Laila said, exhausted: "I don't know. But I will tell you the truth: I am happy I met you. I did not have many friends."
And in that moment, the whispering stopped. And something opened in the air, something you cannot see but can feel, as if the room suddenly grew wider.
"You said it!" shouted the old ifrit. "The word is saying you are happy you met us! The door opens with love, not with spells!"
But the door needed a place to open in. And the place for the door was the wall. The wall that could not bear a door between the two worlds.
"It will fly," said the ifrit in the cap. "The wall will fly when we leave. You must go down from the apartment now and make the people stay away."
"And the people?"
"Don't worry, nothing will happen to anyone. But the wall must go with us. We will take it to a quiet place."

Laila ran down the stairs and knocked on every door: "Get out! Get out quickly!" And people came out in their nightgowns not understanding. And at the moment the last of them stepped out, they heard the sound. A hard sound, from dawn, like a cannon far away.
And the wall vanished. With a ruler, just as people said.

Laila stood in the street and looked at the open apartment. The sun was rising, and the three ifrits stood on the edge waving at her. The old one raised his hand and said in a voice that reached her: "Thank you, Laila. We will keep remembering you."

And since then, my friend, they say that people who come to watch at night, and stand in front of the building and say something kind, anything kind, feel a warm breeze on their faces. Nobody knows why. But the children say: that is the jinn saying hello.
As for Laila, she no longer woke before dawn. But every time she passed the street, she looked at the apartment with no wall, and smiled.

And after the people calmed down, the neighbors sat talking. One woman said she saw a blue light, and a man said he heard children laughing when there were no children. And their old neighbor said: "I have lived here forty years and never saw anything like this." And everyone told the story their own way, and after a week there were ten different versions of the tale, all of them right, and all of them wrong. And that is exactly the beauty of Port Said stories: nobody owns them alone, and everyone adds a piece of themselves.

secs.h: Chapter Nine: Why Does the Story Stay Alive? [حقيقة]
b: This story stays alive because Port Said is full of people who love to tell stories. The city was built by people from everywhere, and each brought a story with them. And the real event, the wall that left its place in 1999, turned from news into an evening out, and from an evening out into a legend.
And there is no place in the world that turns fear into laughter like Port Said. Whoever cannot laugh at the ifrit cannot live here.

[حقيقة] In 1999 a dawn explosion happened in Al-Zohour district in Port Said, and an apartment wall disappeared in a strange way. Residents linked the incident to a story about jinn and "Shams al-Maarif", crowds came to watch, and vendors profited. There is no official explanation and no evidence for the supernatural part, according to the sources.
[خيال] Laila, the three ifrits, the door, and the word that opens it: all of this is our own invention. We used the real story as a background, without accusing or naming any real person.
The story's riddle: the ifrits said the door opens with a simple word. What is it?
1) A secret word from the book  2) Saying you are happy you met them  3) Shouting at the top of your voice
(The right answer: 2.)
Your reward: the "Three Ifrits" card (Rare, No. 002).

3.t: Tennis: The City That Sank Into Stories
3.p: Lake Manzala, Tell Tinnis · Port Said
3.tz: A city once stood in the middle of the water in Lake Manzala. What is left of its story?

secs.h: Chapter One: A City in the Middle of the Water [حقيقة]
b: If you take a boat from Port Said and head into Lake Manzala, after about eight or nine kilometers you will see small mounds rising out of the water. Mounds of brick and dirt, with no house and no tree. But under these mounds, once upon a time, there was a whole city.

Its name was Tinnis. A real city, built on an island in the lake itself, and it flourished most between the ninth and the eleventh centuries AD. It had an important port. Boats entered from the eastern branch of the Nile into the calm water of the lake, waited there until the sea calmed down, and then went out to the Mediterranean. So it was a gate between the Nile and the sea, and between Egypt and faraway lands.

What Tinnis was famous for was textiles. It was known all over the East for the cloth it produced. In the eleventh century, a traveler named Nasir Khusraw visited the city and wrote that it had fifty thousand residents, ten thousand shops and two big Friday mosques. He wrote that most of its people were Copts working in weaving, and that a simple linen shirt could sell for a hundred gold dinars, and an embroidered one could reach thousands.
(Sources 1, 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Two: The Girl and the Thread [خيال]
b: My friend, in that time there was a girl named Mariam, the daughter of an old Coptic weaver. Mariam had something strange: she could hear the thread. The thread being woven would tell her a story.

Every thread on the loom had a small voice, a thin whisper, if someone listened closely. Some threads told about the boats that passed. Some told about the merchants who pulled them tight. And some, if they were the precious kind, the kind made of sea silk, told about the sea itself.

Her father used to say: "We weave, my daughter, we don't tell stories." But Mariam would smile and carry on. And every piece of cloth that came from her hands had a hidden story in it, if anyone knew how to read it.

One day a strange boat stopped in the port of Tinnis, and a tall merchant in a black cloak stepped off with a small bag in his hand. He walked into Mariam's father's workshop and said quietly: "I heard you have a weaver who can hear the thread."
The father was startled: "Who told you?"
"The sea," said the man. "The sea tells a lot."

And he opened the bag and pulled out a thread whose color could not be described. Not blue, not green, not gray, a color like water when the sun sets. "This is a thread of sea silk, from the deepest place in the sea. I want it woven into a single piece. But whoever weaves it must hear what it says."

secs.h: Chapter Four: What the Thread Said [خيال]
b: Mariam sat in front of the loom, took the thread, and brought her ear close. For a moment she heard nothing. And then, suddenly, the voice began. A deep and tired voice, like someone speaking after centuries of silence.
"I am the memory of the sea," said the thread. "Every ship that sank tells me its story, and every sailor who died leaves me his last word. And I carry them all. And I am tired."
"What do you want?" whispered Mariam.
"I want you to weave me. I want someone to keep these stories in cloth, before I forget. The sea forgets, my daughter. We are the ones who remember."

Mariam wove for nights and nights. And every night she heard a new story: about a Phoenician ship, about a sailor who used to sing to his mother, about a whole ship swallowed on a stormy night. And every story went into the cloth, thread by thread, until it became a long piece shining like water under the moon.

secs.h: Chapter Four (continued): The Market of Tinnis [حقيقة وخيال]
b: [حقيقة] To picture the city, imagine that its people lived on the water. Fishing was the basis of their food, and the sources mention different boats: boats for catching fish, boats for catching shrimp, and many kinds of fish like mullet, catfish and tuna. There were special boats for catching the migrating birds that passed over the lake, for food or for export. And people grew wheat and barley on the nearby land.

[خيال] And in the city market, Mariam used to walk with her father on Friday after prayer. The street was crowded, and the merchants called out in every language. One sold spices from India, another sold glass from the Levant. And in a corner of the market, there was an old blind man who sat and told stories to children for a date.
Mariam used to sit beside him and listen. And once she asked him: "Uncle, how do you tell stories without seeing?"
The man laughed: "A story is not seen, my daughter. It is heard. Whoever does not know how to listen loses half the world."
And those words stayed in Mariam's ear for years, and they are what later made her able to hear the thread.

At that time, Tinnis was at the height of its glory. Its cloth sold across the East, and the state watched production and sale strictly, because textiles brought huge profits to the treasury. And fishing was half of people's lives: many kinds of fish and birds were caught from the lake, and they fed the whole city.

But after that time, things began to change. The Crusader wars came to the region, and the coastal cities of the Delta became dangerous. And in the year 1226 AD, the Ayyubid sultan Al-Kamil Muhammad ibn Al-Adil ordered Tinnis to be demolished and destroyed and its people moved out, who numbered about fifty thousand at the time, so that the Crusaders could not seize it and use it as a base. And so the city was erased, leaving behind the mounds you see today.
(Sources 1 and 4 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Six: The Night of Departure [خيال]
b: Now we go back to Mariam. Mariam had grown up, and become an older woman and a famous weaver. And one night her younger brother came running, shouting: "The sultan ordered the city demolished! We have to leave!"

There was no time. People were gathering their belongings and running toward the boats. Mariam stood in the workshop and looked at the piece she had woven from sea silk. It was still hanging on the loom, shining.
"I can't take it," she said. "It's heavy, and the boats won't bear it."
And she heard the voice of the thread, inside the silk: "Don't leave me. If you leave me, the stories will drown."
"So what do I do?"
"Hide me. In a place the sea knows. And I will wait."

Mariam put the cloth in a wooden box, tied it with a rope, and lowered it into the lake water near the shore, in a place she knew. And she said: "I will wait for you, and if I do not come back, someone will come to hear you."

And after the city was demolished, and its people scattered across the Delta and the Levant and everywhere, the box stayed under the water. For years and centuries. And the mounds rose over it, and the lake changed, and the fishermen passed over it without knowing.
But the fishermen say, if you sit in a boat on a calm night and cast your net next to Tell Tinnis, you might hear a voice. The voice of a thread whispering. A story of the sea, coming from below.

secs.h: Chapter Eight: The One Who Heard [خيال]
b: And one night, not long before our own time, there was a young fisherman named Youssef, from Port Said. Youssef was not good at fishing. He would cast his net and sit listening. And on a calm night, he heard.
"Someone will come to hear me," whispered the voice from below.
Youssef was startled and said: "Who is it?"
"I am the memory of the sea. Mariam left me here 800 years ago. But someone has finally come."

Youssef sat in the boat, the lake still, the stars shining on the water. And the thread began to tell. Stories of Tinnis, the city whose story was never told. About the Copts who built the churches, and the fishermen, and those who wove linen worth a hundred dinars, and Mariam who heard the thread.
And before he brought up the box, the thread said: "For me to let you take me, you must solve Mariam's riddle."
And the thread whispered:

(The answer: Tinnis. Game choices: Tinnis, Damietta, Manzala. Review note: the city's name in English, Tennis, is spelled like the sport, so the riddle needs Ahmed's opinion if he finds it hard for Arabs.)
"Tinnis!" said Youssef.

And he heard a long sigh, like decades of tiredness being released. And from under the water, a blue light rose and touched Youssef's hand. And in his hand, suddenly, he found a small thread, its color not a color, like water when the sun sets.

secs.h: Chapter Ten: The Thread's Last Words [خيال]
b: "Tell the story, Youssef," said the thread as it faded. "The city was erased, but the story was not. As long as someone tells about Tinnis, it lives. Even if the water covered it, and the mounds hid it."

And since then, my friend, every time someone from Port Said passes in a boat near Tell Tinnis, they throw a greeting. And they say the thread shines under the water, a tiny gleam, when someone remembers.
And Youssef asked the thread before leaving: "And what will I do with you?"

"Do nothing," said the thread. "Keep me in your pocket, and every time you pass an old place in Port Said, the lighthouse, the port, the markets, bring me close to your ear. You will hear what each place says. I am not only the memory of Tinnis. I am the memory of every place with water."

Youssef put the thread in his pocket, and kept looking at the mounds until the sun rose. And when he got back to land, he told the first person he met the whole story, laughing and crying at once. And the first person he met was a man selling newspapers, who said after he heard it: "That is the best thing I have heard since the day I was born."

[حقيقة] Tinnis was a real city on an island in Lake Manzala, flourishing between the ninth and eleventh centuries, with a port, textiles and fishing. Nasir Khusraw mentioned fifty thousand residents, ten thousand shops and two mosques. And Sultan Al-Kamil ordered it demolished and its people moved out in 1226 because of the Crusader danger. The archaeological mound is about 8 to 9 km from Port Said, and a research project from the University of Exeter is working on it.
[خيال] Mariam, the strange merchant, the talking sea silk, Youssef, and the riddle: our own invention.
Your reward: the "Memory of the Sea" card (Legendary, No. 003).

4.t: Uncle Shehta and the Balma: The Bambouti Who Sold to the Whole World
4.p: Port Said Port, Canal Quay · Port Said
4.tz: Uncle Shehta and the balma on the port quay. The story of the Bambouti who sold to the whole world.

secs.h: Chapter One: Who Is the Bambouti? [حقيقة]
b: Before we tell the story, you need to know who the Bambouti is. The word "bambouti" is one of the most famous words in Port Said, and its origin is English. It comes from the word Boatman, meaning "man of the boat". The locals twisted it their own way until it became bambouti.

The Bambouti is the "sea merchant". He would go out in his small boat to the ships passing through the Suez Canal and sell the sailors on board everything you can imagine: gifts, souvenirs, cloth, and little things to remember Egypt by. They wore a famous hat called the "balma", which became their trademark, so much that people got used to naming the sailors and the Bumboutis after the hat itself.

And because the Bambouti dealt with every nationality passing through the canal, he needed no diplomas. He learned the language from the sailors themselves. He took a word from English, a word from French and a word from Greek, and twisted them until they became his own word. That is how many expressions entered the language of Port Said's people, because the city was built by people coming from everywhere.
(Sources 1 and 2 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Two: Uncle Shehta Wakes Up [خيال]
b: My friend, one morning Uncle Shehta woke to the sound of the sea. Uncle Shehta was a third generation Bambouti, his father was a Bambouti and his grandfather was a Bambouti, and each of them passed down the boat, the balma and the tongue.

Uncle Shehta's tongue was a story all by itself. Say it was longer than the canal and you would hardly be exaggerating. He could sell water to a fish, and convince a shark it needed a toothbrush. It was said he once sold a wall clock to a captain, telling him: "Look, boss, this clock counts the moments you have left in life." And the captain bought it, scared.
And he put on his balma, looked in the mirror, and told himself: "Today is a big day. Today I will sell to the biggest ship that ever passed through the canal."
Uncle Shehta stood on the quay and looked at the canal. A huge ship was coming from far away, black and big like a floating building. And a small tug was pulling it slowly.
"That one is mine!" said Uncle Shehta as he ran toward his boat. "Boys, load the goods!"

And his two sons, Hassanein and Zeinhom, ran after him. Hassanein was young and naughty, and Zeinhom was older and thought a lot. They carried the boxes from the house: little pharaoh statues stamped "Made in Port Said", galabiyas, slippers, and the Hagg's tea glass.
"Father," said Hassanein, carrying a box, "what are these statues for?"
"They are for the best business in the world," said Uncle Shehta as he threw the boat rope. "Tourists love pharaohs. Pharaohs never get upset, and never ask for money."

Uncle Shehta's boat came alongside the ship, and he and his sons climbed up the ropes. The captain was standing above, a tall dark man in black sunglasses, looking over the deck. When he saw Uncle Shehta, he raised an eyebrow.
"What is this?"
"Welcome, boss!" said Uncle Shehta in broken English. "Welcome to Port Said! I have the best things in the world, everything handmade, almost free!"
The captain did not understand half of it, but he understood that this man would not leave him alone. So he smiled and said: "My friend, what the price?"
"Price?" laughed Uncle Shehta. "For a friend, free. But if you want to pay, I won't refuse!"
And that was the beginning of the longest negotiation in the history of the canal.

Uncle Shehta kept showing his goods for two full hours. He brought out a little Sphinx statue and said: "This is original, from the days of King Khufu himself." He brought out a galabiya and said: "This is Egyptian cotton, it warms you in winter and cools you in summer." He brought out a slipper and said: "This is a pharaonic slipper, made for Cleopatra."
"Cleopatra wore slippers?" asked the captain in a surprised voice.
"Of course, boss! She was a queen, she had to be comfortable."
Hassanein and Zeinhom stood behind him holding in their laughter. And Zeinhom whispered to his brother: "Your father could sell air to a drowning man."
"Yes," whispered Hassanein, "and take a tip for it."
And in the end, the captain bought two statues and a galabiya, and said: "You are the best seller I ever met."
"I am not a seller, boss," said Uncle Shehta proudly, "I am a Bambouti."

But at that moment, they heard the sound of another boat approaching. Another boat full of goods, and on it a man wearing a balma tilted to one side, shouting from far away: "Boss! Don't buy from him! I have better!"
"That is Farghaly," whispered Uncle Shehta through his teeth. "My rival since our youth."
And Farghaly climbed onto the ship, laughing: "Shehta! Still selling fake statues?"
"Fake? These are original! I carved them with my own hands yesterday!"
"So only since yesterday?"

The captain stood between the two of them not understanding anything, and looked at Hassanein and Zeinhom, who were trying to hide their laughter. And finally the captain said in English in a tired voice: "Can someone explain to me what is going on?"
And the two answered together, at the same moment, in the same tone: "Business, boss. Business."
And the captain laughed for the first time in two hours, and said: "I will buy from both of you."

And then, my friend, it turned out Farghaly and Shehta were friends since childhood, and that this fight is staged in front of every customer to make a story. And that they split the profits in half at the end. That is the secret of Port Said, my friend: even the fight is sold.

secs.h: Chapter Six (prelude): The Language of the Bambouti [حقيقة وخيال]
b: [حقيقة] The sources say that the Bumboutis, because they dealt with every nationality in the world, learned to speak by twisting words: they take the foreign word and change it until it fits their pronunciation. And from here came part of the everyday language of Port Said's people.
[خيال] And Uncle Shehta used to tell his sons: "Language is like tea, kids. If you leave it alone in the glass, it goes cold. You have to stir it with your hand, and put in sugar from every country."
And Zeinhom, who always thought, would ask: "And how do we know the right word?"
"There is no right word," Uncle Shehta would answer. "There is a word that makes the customer smile."
And after they finished selling, Uncle Shehta and his sons got back down into the small boat. The father was quiet, unlike his usual self, watching the ship move away.
"What is it, Father?" asked Zeinhom.

"I am thinking," said Uncle Shehta. "This ship passed here and will go to very faraway lands. And on it is a statue from Port Said, a galabiya from Port Said, and a story from Port Said. And from today in a country at the end of the world someone will see this statue and say: this is a gift from Egypt."
"And what is important about that?"

"What is important, my son," said Uncle Shehta, "is that we don't only sell goods. We sell Port Said. Every ship that passes takes a piece of us. And this city was built that way, without anyone planning it. Small people working with their hands, and each of them carrying Egypt to a faraway country."

And in Port Said, the Bumboutis had a life beyond work. They had a dance called the "Bambouti dance", done to the tunes of the simsimiyya, and it appears in the celebrations of the canal cities. People hold the simsimiyya in their hands and play happy tunes, swaying in the streets. And the songs are sung with words from the heart of daily life.

And in a famous song from the heritage, it says: "I am a Port Saidi and a Bambouti, and I sell goods from Asyut, and I love the people of the Qabouti." And all of it tells of pride in the profession and the city.
(Sources 3 and 4 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Eight: The Night of Celebration [خيال]
b: That night, Uncle Shehta decided to celebrate. He brought his grandfather's old simsimiyya, and invited all the neighbors. And he sat on the quay, night falling, a small fire lit, and tea going around.

He began to play, and the tune of the simsimiyya rose with the wind. And people gathered. And the dance began. Hassanein and Zeinhom got up from among the people, their balmas on their heads, and began to sway the way they learned from their father.

And in the middle of the dance, a strange man appeared on the quay, wearing old sailor clothes. He stood watching with a smile. And after the song ended, he came up to Uncle Shehta and said quietly: "Are you Uncle Shehta?"
"Yes?"
"I am the captain of the ship. I came back to tell you that the statue you sold me sits in my office, and every time someone visits me, I tell them about Port Said."
Uncle Shehta laughed and said: "Boss, come drink tea with us. But before that, I have a riddle for you. If you solve it, the tea is free."
"Free? That is great generosity. Go ahead."
(The answer: Bambouti. Game choices: Bambouti, sailor, captain. Original meaning: Boatman.)
"Bambouti!" said the captain without thinking.
"Bravo!" shouted Uncle Shehta. "The tea is free, and the second tea is half price!"

secs.h: Chapter Ten: The Point of the Story
b: And they kept talking until dawn. Uncle Shehta told about his grandfather, and his father, and the boats, and the captain told about faraway lands. And in the end, before going to sleep, the captain said: "I learned something from you today."
"What is it?"
"That trade is not only money. Trade is a story."
And Uncle Shehta smiled, put the balma on his head, and said: "That is what every Bambouti has said since the day it began."

And before the captain left that night, young Hassanein asked him: "Will you come back?" And the captain looked at him and said: "Every time the ship passes here, I will come up on the quay and look for a balma tilted a little." Uncle Shehta laughed and said: "That is Farghaly's balma, mine is straight!" And everyone laughed until dawn came. And years later, when Hassanein grew up and became a Bambouti too, whenever he climbed onto a new ship, the first sentence he said was: "Welcome to Port Said. Tea is on us."
[حقيقة] The Bambouti is a real sea merchant, the origin of the word is Boatman, the balma is their famous hat, and the dance and the song are part of Port Said's heritage.
[خيال] Uncle Shehta, Hassanein, Zeinhom, the captain, and the negotiation: our own invention.
Your reward: the "Uncle Shehta" card (Common, No. 004).

5.t: The Singing Nadaha: The Story of the Simsimiyya
5.tz: On the Corniche at night there is a voice singing. Is it a Nadaha or a simsimiyya?

b: When you hear the word "Nadaha" in Egyptian folk stories, you might picture a mysterious woman calling people at night, so they follow her voice and never come back. But in Port Said, the Nadaha means something else entirely. The Nadaha here is the simsimiyya.

The simsimiyya is a folk instrument tied to the canal cities, especially Port Said. They call it "the Nadaha" or "the Nadha" because whoever hears its tune is enchanted by its sound, and walks after it searching here and there, until he reaches the place of the celebration, and stands to listen and join the people.

And the sources say the women of Port Said were its first lovers. It was not just a musical instrument, it was for them a support in war and in peace. They would tell it: "Sing, Simsim," and it would sing.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Two: The Story of Al-Naggi (circulating account)
b: And the story says, according to what the elders tell, that the simsimiyya came to the canal from far away. In the days of digging the Suez Canal, between 1859 and 1869, a Nubian folk artist named Mohamed Osman Al-Naggi traveled from Nubia to the canal region, carrying an instrument called the tanbura. The tanbura is the great mother of the simsimiyya, it has eight strings, and it resembles the ancient pharaonic harp.

And this Al-Naggi, according to the account, is the one who planted the first seed of the simsimiyya art in the three canal cities. And in the old simsimiyya songs, there is a famous line that says: "Thank God he came."

And later in the thirties came another artist named Abdullah Kobarber, called "the Nubian magician", who lived his life like a journey with no end, and helped spread the instrument. And then, in the fifties, the simsimiyya developed at the hands of the artist Hassan Metwally, who is said to be the true pioneer of the national simsimiyya movement. And they say many famous people loved it, like Ismail Yassin and Shakoko.
(Sources 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: The Boy Who Listened [خيال]
b: Now we leave the books and tell a story. One night, there was a boy named Omar, thirteen years old, living in the old quarter of Port Said. Omar was sad. His father had gone to work on a ship for months, his mother was busy, and his friends played on their phones and did not talk.

Omar left the house at night and walked along the Corniche, the wind cold, the stars few. And suddenly he heard a sound. A small tune, like someone plucking a string in the air. Tan... tan... tan... and then another tune, sweeter.

Omar stopped. He looked around. There was nobody. But the tune was calling him. And he felt something pulling him, not forcefully, but gently, the way his mother used to pull him by the hand when he was little.

Omar followed the sound, along the Corniche, until he reached a small closed kiosk, and beside it sat an old woman on a wooden chair. She wore a black galabiya, a white scarf on her head, and in her lap a small instrument with eight strings.
"Welcome, Omar," she said without looking at him.
Omar was startled: "Do you know me?"
"I know everyone the simsimiyya calls," said the woman with a smile. "My name is Umm Saad. Sit."

Omar sat on the pavement, still not understanding. And the woman said as she adjusted a string: "This simsimiyya is no ordinary instrument. It listens. If you are sad, it will call you. If you are happy, it will sing with you. And if you are lonely, it will sit beside you."
"And me?" asked Omar in a low voice.
"You are lonely," said Umm Saad. "And sad about your father."
Omar gasped: "How did you know?"
"The simsimiyya told me." And Umm Saad played a simple tune and sang in a deep voice:

And Omar felt the words enter his chest and settle there in the place of the sadness. And his eyes teared up without meaning to. And Umm Saad finished the song, the tune of the simsimiyya wrapping around them like a shawl.

"This used to be said long ago for those at sea," said Umm Saad when she finished. "The women would sit on the shore and sing, and the boats would listen. To this day they say that whoever sings to the sea, the sea delivers it."

secs.h: Chapter Five (continued): The Women on the Shore [خيال]
b: Umm Saad was quiet for a bit, and looked at the sea. And then she said: "Do you know what is not told in books?"
"What?"

"That the women held a gathering on the shore every Thursday night. Each one brought something to eat and something to sing. They sat in a circle, the simsimiyya in the middle, and the songs passed from one woman to the next like tea. And we little ones sat behind and listened and learned."
"And your father?" asked Omar.

"My father was a sailor," she said with a nostalgic smile. "And he was gone for months. And my mother and I sang for him every night. And after a year he came back and told my mother he heard our voices in the middle of the sea on a stormy night, and that he found his way back from the song."
"Is that true?"
"I don't know," laughed Umm Saad. "But what I know is that he came back."
And Omar looked at the water. And he thought of his father. And he wished his father would hear a tune somewhere, and that it would bring him home.

secs.h: Chapter Six: War and the Simsimiyya [حقيقة]
b: And in the days of war, the simsimiyya was something else. The sources say it played an important role in the years of the War of Attrition, and was one of the strongest tools of popular media. The simple people of the canal used it to ignite patriotism and resistance among the people. And the women would tell it: "Sing, Simsim," and it sang for the cannons and for every strong hand protecting the country.

And to this day, in Port Said, the simsimiyya is part of celebrations, weddings and family occasions, and on ordinary nights too. And there are bands still working today, like the band of Reis Zakaria, who preserve the heritage and tell the background of each song before singing it.
(Sources 1 and 4 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Seven: The Seven Forts (circulating account)
b: And they say the simsimiyya became famous from inside a cafe in Port Said called "The Seven Forts", and that many people used to come to hear it there. And that this was the beginning of the bands and sessions that later became organized work.
[خيال] And Umm Saad told Omar: "Back then, I used to sit in that cafe as a child, under the tables, and listen. Girls were not allowed to sit, but the simsimiyya let me sit without anyone noticing."
Omar laughed: "So you were a sneak?"
"I was the best sneak in the neighborhood," said Umm Saad with a wink. "And every night I learned a new word from the songs."
And after they finished talking, Umm Saad said: "Do you want to try?"
"Me? I don't know how to play."

"Nobody does the first time," she said, and put the simsimiyya in his lap. "The simsimiyya is not learned with the hand. It is learned with the ear. Listen first, and then your hand will find its way on its own."

Omar put his fingers on the strings. The first note came out off key, like a cat's meow. Umm Saad laughed until she cried. The second note, a little better. And on the third note, Omar stopped and said: "Did you hear that?"
"I heard," said Umm Saad. "That is your voice."

And Omar kept playing. One note after another, slowly and stumbling, but with an honest sound. And far off, on the water, he saw a small boat passing, and a fisherman in it raising his hand to say hello. And with him another man waving a scarf.
And Umm Saad said as she took the simsimiyya from him: "Before you go, a riddle. If you solve it, the simsimiyya will remember you all your life."
(The answer: the simsimiyya. Game choices: the simsimiyya, the oud, the rababa.)
"The simsimiyya!" said Omar.
And Umm Saad smiled, and at that moment, a tune came out of the strings by itself without anyone touching them. A long, warm note, and then it fell silent.
Omar went home after midnight. And in the house a light was on. His mother was sitting in front of the phone, crying. "Where were you? I was worried!"
"I was listening to something beautiful," said Omar.
And at that moment, the phone rang. It was his father, from the ship, from the middle of the sea. "Hello, Omar? I had a strange dream. I dreamed I heard a simsimiyya and you were playing."
Omar opened his mouth and could not speak. He looked at his mother, and she looked at him, and they both laughed with eyes full of tears.

And weeks later, when the father came back from his trip, the first thing he asked Omar was: "Play me what I dreamed of." Omar sat next to his father on the Corniche, held a small simsimiyya he bought with his allowance, and played one note, not complete, and not very beautiful. But the father closed his eyes and smiled, and said: "That is the same tune." And Umm Saad from far away, sitting on her chair, raised her hand and waved, and then disappeared with the wind the way she came.

And since then, they say Omar goes out every Thursday night to the Corniche. And that from a small closed kiosk you can hear a tune. And that whoever sits next to it and listens may feel that someone is calling them. Someone saying: "Don't be sad. Someone is listening to you."

[حقيقة] The simsimiyya is a folk instrument tied to Port Said and the canal cities, and it is called "the Nadaha". According to a circulating account, it entered the canal with the digging of the canal (1859 to 1869) at the hands of the Nubian Mohamed Osman Al-Naggi with the tanbura instrument, and Kobarber and Hassan Metwally were pioneers of the instrument in the twentieth century. It played a role in national songs and in war and celebration. And bands like the band of Reis Zakaria are still working.
[خيال] Omar, Umm Saad, the kiosk, the phone call, and the riddle: all of this is our own invention. And the song "Ya Bahr Ya Wasa'" we wrote ourselves, it is not from the heritage.
Your reward: the "Umm Saad" card (Legendary, No. 005).

6.t: The Empty Standing One: The Story of the Waiting Pedestal
6.p: Pedestal of the de Lesseps Statue, Canal Entrance · Port Said
6.tz: An empty pedestal at the canal entrance, and someone is still waiting for it. Who is it, and why?

secs.h: Chapter One: A Pedestal Without a Statue [حقيقة]
b: If you walk along the old quay at the canal entrance in Port Said, you will see something strange: a tall stone pedestal with nothing on it. An empty pedestal. Standing in its place as if waiting for someone.

This pedestal used to carry a statue of Ferdinand de Lesseps, the French engineer whose name is tied to digging the Suez Canal. The statue and the pedestal were made in 1899 to celebrate thirty years since the canal opened to navigation. The pedestal stood at the entrance of the old tourist quay, on the west bank of the canal.

And in 1956, when the British-French attack on Port Said happened, the angry locals removed the statue in protest. Since then the pedestal has been empty. As for the statue itself, they say it was moved to a place in the shipbuilding yard in Port Fouad.
(Sources 1, 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Two: Port Said Before the Pedestal [حقيقة]
b: To understand why this pedestal matters, we have to go back to the beginning of the city. Port Said was founded on April 25, 1859, during the digging of the canal, when de Lesseps struck the first symbolic blow with a pickaxe. And the city had nothing in it. The sources say everything had to be brought from outside: wood, stone, equipment, houses, food, even water.

The first houses came ready-made in crates, and were built of wood. And the quay itself was built with a new kind of concrete called "Beton Coignet", named after its inventor. In the early days there were only 150 workers, sleeping in tents around a wooden hut.
So the place where the statue once stood was first sand and water, and from workers and pickaxes a city came out.

secs.h: Chapter Three: The Morning Without a Statue [خيال]
b: Let us tell a story. One morning, there was a little boy named Yassin, eight years old, walking along the quay with his grandfather. Yassin was curious, and asked about everything.
"Grandpa," he said, pointing to the pedestal, "what is that?"
"That is a place where a statue used to be, Yassin."
"And where did the statue go?"
"It went on a trip," said the grandfather with a smile.
"And won't it come back?"
The grandfather was quiet a bit, and looked at the pedestal. Then he said: "We don't know. But the pedestal is still waiting for it."
Yassin stood in front of the pedestal and looked at it for a long time. And he felt something strange. He felt the pedestal was looking back at him, and was sad.

secs.h: Chapter Four: The Empty Standing One [خيال]
b: And at night, when the street was quiet, Yassin woke to a faint sound. He jumped out of bed and went to the window. And he saw on the quay, under the floodlights, the shadow of a man standing on the pedestal.
Not a real man. A shadow. Transparent like smoke, wearing an old suit and a hat, with his hand behind his back. Standing silent and looking at the canal.
Yassin went down on tiptoe and walked up to the pedestal. The shadow did not move. Yassin said in a low voice: "Who are you?"
The shadow slowly turned his head and looked at him. He had no features, but he had a voice, an old and distant voice: "I am the one who used to stand here. But I no longer remember who I am."
"Are you the statue?"
"I am what is left of him," said the shadow. "His shadow."
Yassin sat on the quay, and the shadow sat beside him, without the air moving. And the shadow began to speak in a tired voice:

"I have stood here for a very long time. I used to think my place was here, and that I was guarding the canal. But one day, people came and took the statue away, and left the pedestal. And I stayed. I did not know where to go."
"Are you sad?" asked Yassin.
"I don't know. Sometimes I feel I don't want to leave, because I love the view. And sometimes I feel the people were right, and that what was here was not theirs."
And he was quiet a while. Then: "But the problem is I don't know who I am without the statue. I mean, who am I if I was not embodied in stone?"
And Yassin, who was eight, thought for a moment and said something unexpected: "You are not a statue, mister. You are someone who looks at the canal. And you love the view. That is enough."

secs.h: Chapter Six: The One Who Watches the Boats [خيال]
b: The shadow let out a soft laugh. "Someone who looks at the canal. That is the best definition I have heard."

And the two of them sat on the quay, the boy and the shadow, watching the ships. Big ships passing slowly in the dark, each lit like a small city. And with each ship that passed, the shadow told about it: "This one comes from very far. This one carries wheat. This one carries people who want to see Port Said."
"You know everything!" said Yassin.
"I have stood here a long time," said the shadow. "Whoever stands in one place sees everything that passes."
And they stayed sitting until the color of the sky began to change. And at that moment, the shadow said: "I have a riddle for you, Yassin. If you solve it, I will tell you a secret."
And suddenly a big seagull landed on the edge of the pedestal, looked at the shadow with one eye, and said in a hoarse voice: "You again? You sit here every night and scare the tourists!"
"I scare nobody," answered the shadow with dignity. "I just stand."
"On my pedestal!" shrieked the seagull. "I have slept on it for ten years."
Yassin laughed until he fell onto the quay. "You two are fighting over the pedestal?"
"We have fought for ages," said the shadow with a shrug. "He says the pedestal is his, and I say it is mine. And in the end we both stay."
"So what is the solution?"
"The solution," said the seagull arrogantly, "is that whoever comes in the morning is the one who stands. And whoever comes at night leaves the place."
And the shadow adjusted his hat and said: "That is a fair deal, kids. But I don't sleep, so I come at night and leave before dawn. And he comes in the morning. And so each of us has his shift."

And Yassin sat laughing at an independent state of a shadow and a seagull sharing a stone pedestal. And he told himself: if what is happening here is ifrits, then Port Said is the loveliest city in the world for ifrits.

And then, my friend, the seagull began to tell stories too. And it turned out he knew many stories about the ships, because he follows the vessels from the start of the canal to its end. About a man who forgot his glasses on a ship's deck and searched for them for months, and about a ship that arrived with a cat that walked the whole quay looking for its owner. Small stories, but each had warmth in it.
(The answer: the de Lesseps pedestal. Game choices: the lighthouse, the de Lesseps pedestal, the Canal Authority dome. Hint: the year 1899.)
"The pedestal!" said Yassin quickly. "You are an empty pedestal, but not empty, because it has a story in it."
The shadow smiled. And for the first time, his face began to show a little, faint features. "Bravo, Yassin."

"The secret," said the shadow, "is that what remains after the statue goes is not the stone. It is the story. The statue can be taken, and the pedestal can stay empty, but if someone sits beside it and tells another what happened, the pedestal is full."
"Full of what?"
"Of people who remember. Of everyone who passes and asks: what is that? And someone answers."
Yassin stood and looked at the pedestal, and found that it really did look different. Not empty, but waiting. Waiting for children to ask, and grandfathers to tell.
"Tomorrow I will bring my friends," said Yassin. "And we will tell them."
"And I will sit here," said the shadow, "and I won't be sad."

And let me tell you something else, from the facts. In Port Said, people have a special relationship with history. The city was built by many people from all over the world, and in the early twentieth century it was one of the most diverse cities in the world. And the writer Rudyard Kipling said a famous sentence about it: if you want to find someone you know who is traveling, there are two places in the world where you only need to sit and wait, and in the end he will come: the quays of London and Port Said.

And at the same time, this city values its dignity. And in 1956, when it was attacked, its people took a historic stand, and removing the statue was part of their response. And the empty pedestal turned from a piece of decoration into something that tells a position.
(Sources 1, 4 and 5 at the end of the file.)
Yassin grew up and became a man. And every time he passed the quay and saw the pedestal, he stopped a moment and smiled. And once his small son came with him, and asked: "Dad, what is that?"
Yassin looked at the pedestal, and in the light of sunset he saw something shining on its edge: a faint shadow, waving its hand.
"That, my dear," said Yassin, "is a place with a story. Sit, and I will tell it to you."
And the two of them sat on the quay, the ships passing, the pedestal standing in its place, not empty.

And since then, whenever Yassin walks on the quay with any strange child, he stops him in front of the pedestal and asks the same question: "What do you see?" And every child answers differently. One says: "A stone." A girl says: "A place for a statue." And a little boy once said: "It looks sad." And Yassin would smile every time, because he knew every answer was right, and that a pedestal that hears all these answers is not empty at all.

[حقيقة] The de Lesseps statue pedestal really exists at the entrance of the old tourist quay, made in 1899 for the thirtieth anniversary of the canal opening, and the statue was removed in 1956 after the attack, and the pedestal has been empty since. Port Said was founded in 1859, and all its building materials were brought from outside.
[خيال] Yassin, the grandfather, the shadow, and all the dialogue: our own invention. We used the shadow as a symbol of memory, without any political interpretation.
Your reward: the "Empty Standing One" card (Rare, No. 006).

7.t: The Three Domes: The Ones Who Count the Ships
7.p: Suez Canal Authority Building, the Green Domes · Port Said
7.tz: Three green domes above the canal building. What exactly are they counting?

secs.h: Chapter One: The First Thing That Comes to Mind [حقيقة]
b: If you ask anyone about Port Said, the first picture that comes to mind is probably the Suez Canal Authority building. A big building on the canal bank, looking like a palace, with three green domes shining in the sun above it.

This building was built in 1895 in the reign of Khedive Abbas Hilmi II. It was built directly on the canal bank, and its purpose was to follow the movement of the ships passing through. It looks like a palace in the Islamic style, and that shows in the three green domes, in the decorations of the ceilings and walls inside, and in the windows and chandeliers that adorn the interior.
And the sources say a French construction company built it, but no one knows precisely who the engineer was who designed it. So even this famous building has a small secret.
(Sources 1 and 2 at the end of the file.)

And this building has seen important moments in Egypt's history. From the sources, it is among the registered monuments in Port Said, and it witnessed the raising of the Egyptian flag by President Gamal Abdel Nasser after the British forces left Egypt in 1956, announcing Egypt's regaining of full sovereignty.
So the building does not only follow ships. It is a place where a lot of history sat, and it has been in the pictures made of Port Said ever since.

secs.h: Chapter Three: The Girl Who Counts [خيال]
b: Now let us tell a story. There was a girl named Huda, twelve years old, who loved to count. She counted anything: the pigeons on the roof, the cars in the street, the tiles on the pavement. And she had a strange hobby: every day after school she would sit on the Corniche opposite the canal building and count the ships passing.
"Twenty three," she would say as she wrote in a small notebook. "Twenty four."
And one day, while she sat counting, she heard a voice coming from above, from the building. A soft voice, like a woman speaking from behind a curtain.
"Twenty four... wrong."
Huda raised her head. There was nobody. But the voice said again: "We counted twenty five."

Huda got up and went closer to the building. She stood in front of the stairs and looked up toward the domes. And at that moment, she felt the green domes move a little, like someone adjusting their seat.
"Who are you?" she asked in a trembling voice.
"We are the domes," said a voice from above. "I am the big one, and my name is Nagma. This is my middle sister, her name is Hilal. And the little one is called Badr."

The three appeared in the sky above the building, three small ladies in green dresses like the domes. Nagma was tall and serious, Hilal was cheerful and laughed at anything, and Badr was small and naughty and bounced on the head of the dome.
"We have counted the ships since the day we were built," said Nagma. "Every ship that passes, we record it in a big notebook. But you counted wrong today."
"How?"
"You missed a ship," said Hilal laughing. "Behind the big oil tanker there was a small ship hiding."

The three sisters came down from the domes and stood in front of Huda. And Nagma pulled from her dress pocket a huge notebook, bigger than a school book, and opened it to a page full of numbers and names.

"This is our notebook," she said. "Since 1895 we have been writing in it. Every ship that passed: its name, from what country, and what it carries. And we also write something small about each one, something nobody cares about."
"Like what?"

"Like that there was a ship from Japan carrying a cat that got off in Port Said for a walk and left the captain waiting. And another ship whose passengers sang the whole way. And a third whose captain cried every time he passed here, out of joy at seeing the light of the country."
And Huda looked at the notebook not believing it. "This is the loveliest notebook I have ever seen."
"And you are the loveliest girl who counts," said Badr laughing. "But you still count wrong."
And Hilal decided to hold a contest. "Who counts ships better? Huda or us?"
"Me?" said Huda. "I can't compete with you, you have been counting for 120 years."
"But you have something we don't," said Nagma. "You have an eye that sees from below. We see from above, and the ships look small. You see them big."

They sat competing. Each time a ship passed, Huda said her number, and the three sisters said theirs. And the competition was fierce, until a huge ship appeared, black like a mountain, and passed slowly. And they all went quiet to watch.
"Every time a ship like this passes," whispered Nagma, "I feel the canal breathing."

secs.h: Chapter Six (continued): The Story of the Japanese Cat [خيال]
b: "Tell us about the cat," said Huda as she sat on the stairs. "The one that got off in Port Said."

Hilal smiled, happy that someone asked. "It was a ship coming from Japan, and on it was a small white cat that slept on the ropes. And every day the captain gave her a fish. And one night the ship stopped in front of us to wait its turn in the canal. And suddenly the cat jumped off the rope, landed on the quay, and walked toward the city."
"And where did she go?"

"She went to the restaurant at the start of the street, and kept meowing until the cook came out to her. And he was cooking fish. And the cat went up and ate. And the ship waited an hour, and the captain stood at the rail calling: Biso, Biso!"
"And then?"
"The cat came back after she finished, and climbed onto the ship without a word, as if she had been on a normal outing. And the captain laughed until he fell on the floor."
"That was the longest hour in the history of the notebook," said Hilal. "And we wrote beside it: the cat has a more important schedule than the captain."
And Huda laughed until she cried. And she said: "You are the loveliest residents of any building."

secs.h: Chapter Seven (prelude): The Night of Lights [خيال]
b: And before the night ended, the three sisters decided to show Huda something they do once a year. They blew on themselves, and turned into a soft green light, and rose to the sky above the building. And in a moment, the whole street changed. The pavements were covered in green light, the water in the canal shone, and the passing ships looked as if they were swimming in a sea of emerald.
Huda stood with her mouth open. "This... this is so beautiful."
"This is the thank you," said Nagma in a voice coming from the sky. "Every year on this night, we say thank you to everyone who stood and watched us. Even if they did not know we exist."
And Huda stood until the light disappeared. And she went home feeling she had seen the loveliest thing in her life, and that nobody would believe her, and that she did not care.

secs.h: Chapter Seven: The Other Side of the Domes [حقيقة]
b: And let me tell you something real about the building. This building is not only a beautiful shape, it really was a place for following ships in the canal. And its Islamic design, with the domes and decorations, was a striking choice in a city whose architecture was mostly built in the European style. So among the wooden houses and the European balconies, there is a building reminding you that this city also stands on Egyptian land.

And one nice piece of information is that the Suez Canal Authority still uses the building. And that people have come for generations to take pictures in front of it. And it is among the most famous pictures of Port Said in the world.
(Source 3 at the end of the file.)
And before Huda left, Nagma said: "We have a custom. Whoever counts with the domes must solve a riddle."
(The answer: the Suez Canal Authority building. Game choices: the lighthouse, the Suez Canal Authority building, Simon Arzt.)
"You!" shouted Huda. "The building you live on top of!"
Badr clapped as she bounced: "She solved it! She solved it!"
And Nagma opened a new page in the big notebook, and wrote at its top: "Huda, counts the ships."
"But I am not a ship," laughed Huda.
"You are a story," said Nagma. "And every story is recorded."

And from then on, when Huda sat counting ships, she felt something moving above the building. And she would wave her hand and say: "Good morning Nagma. Good morning Hilal. Good morning Badr." And every time she felt the domes shine a little brighter.

And one night, years later, when Huda became a tour guide and was telling visitors about the building, she said: "This is a building with three domes." And a small child at the back of the group corrected her: "No, those are three sisters."
And Huda smiled. "You are right."

And before she left, Huda asked: "Will you stay here forever?" And Nagma looked at the canal and said: "As long as ships pass, we will keep counting. But if someone stands in front of the building and says good morning, we will answer them. Even if they do not hear." And Huda smiled, because she knew this is what it means to not be alone in the city, and that there are people sitting above, counting, and remembering.

[حقيقة] The Suez Canal Authority building in Port Said was built in 1895 in the reign of Khedive Abbas Hilmi II, in the shape of an Islamic palace with three green domes, to follow ship movement. A French company built it and the engineer is not known precisely. It is among the registered monuments, and witnessed the raising of the Egyptian flag in 1956 after the evacuation.
[خيال] Huda, the dome sisters (Nagma, Hilal and Badr), the big notebook, and the contest: our own invention.
Your reward: the "Three Domes" card (Rare, No. 007).
