8.t: Simon Arzt: The Ceiling That Told Stories in Colors
8.p: Simon Arzt, Palestine Street on the Canal · Port Said
8.tz: An old ceiling on Palestine Street tells stories in colors. What is painted on it?

secs.h: Chapter One: The Store Built for Sailors [حقيقة]
b: On Palestine Street, facing the Suez Canal, stands an old building called Simon Arzt. The building's official website says it was the first mall in Egypt and the second oldest mall in the world (that is the website's own claim while marketing the place, not a neutral judgment). But what is certain is that it was a big store with everything in it.

Simon Arzt was originally a grocery and tobacco store, built specifically for sailors and travelers passing through the canal. And its owner, according to the website, was a man named Simon Arzt, a Turkish Jewish tobacco farmer, who arrived in Port Said in 1869, the year the canal opened, to invest his money in Egypt. He set up tobacco factories in Cairo and Alexandria between 1907 and 1913, and then came to Port Said and built the big store facing the canal and named it after himself.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Two: A House of Glass [حقيقة]
b: The building was designed in the European style, like the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II in Milan and Naples. Its area is two thousand square meters, and its facade is forty meters. Inside is a rectangular hall with exhibits on two floors.
And the most beautiful thing in it was the ceiling. A ceiling of colored glass, with light entering from every side. And on the inner floors, a wrought iron railing runs along the balconies.

On the date of construction, the official website says it was built in 1922 and the store opened in 1923. But the Port Said governorate website says it opened in 1932, so the sources disagree. In our story we will say "in the twenties" to leave the matter open.
(Sources 1, 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: Salma and the Ceiling [خيال]
b: Back to the story. One year, there was a girl named Salma, eight years old, coming to the store with her mother for the first time. Salma loved colors. Anything colorful drew her: sweets, dresses, balloons.

She walked into the store and raised her head, and stopped. Because above her was the glass ceiling, and light was coming through it in color, red and blue and green and yellow, drawing patterns on the floor like drawings from a dream.
"Mama!" she pulled her mother's hand. "Look, the ceiling is drawing!"
"It is not drawing, sweetheart, it is glass."
"No," said Salma stubbornly. "It is drawing."
And she kept standing and watching it, while people passed around her and her mother browsed the cloth.

secs.h: Chapter Four: What Was in the Glass [خيال]
b: And suddenly Salma heard a whisper coming from above. A thin whisper like the sound of a small bell. "Can you see us?"

And she looked up, and found in every color of the glass someone sitting. In the red, a little ifrit in a cap. In the blue, a mermaid. In the green, a boy holding a leaf. And in the yellow, a small sun smiling.
"We are the colors of the glass," said the mermaid. "We have lived here since the store was built. And every day we try to tell our stories to people, but nobody looks up."
"I looked up!" said Salma proudly.
"Yes," said the red ifrit. "You are the first child to look up in 20 years."

secs.h: Chapter Five: The Red Ifrit's Story [خيال]
b: Salma sat on the floor, her mother still busy. And the red ifrit said: "Would you like us to tell you the first story?"
"Yes!"

"Long ago, when the store was built, there was a man named Simon. An older man with a white mustache. And he loved sailors, because he built the store for them. And every time a new sailor arrived, Simon would tell him: buy what you want, and if you have no money, pay me with a story."
"A story?" said Salma.

"Yes. He used to say the best thing a person can buy from a foreign land is a story to carry back to their own country. So the sailors would tell him about their cities and families, and he would record the stories in a notebook, and write the sailor's name beside them."
And the ifrit was quiet and looked at the glass. "And when Simon died, the notebook stayed. And the stories went into the glass. And we became their characters."

"And me?" asked the blue mermaid in her thin voice. "I am from the story of a Greek sailor. He brought Simon a big shell and told him: my mother's voice is in it. And the sailor was crying as he told it, because it had been years since he saw his mother. And Simon put the shell in the store and told him: when you pass next time, you will find it."
"And did he come?" asked Salma.

"Yes," said the mermaid. "Two years later. And he saw the shell in its place. And he cried again. And then he heard his mother's voice, not from the shell, but coming from behind him. Because she had come with him this time."
And Salma stayed quiet. And said: "That is beautiful."

"More than beautiful," said the green boy. "But a lot is said about this ceiling. Some people say Simon wished to build a ceiling that made people feel they were in paradise. And some say the ceiling itself asked for that."

secs.h: Chapter Six (continued): The Green Boy and the Market [خيال]
b: "And as for me," said the green boy, raising the leaf in his hand, "I am from a sweeter story."
"Tell it!"

"One day, a very tall Norwegian sailor walked into the store, his head bumping the lamps. He wanted to buy a gift for his daughter, but did not know what his daughter liked. He stood in front of the shelves and looked for a full hour. And Simon came and asked him: how old is your daughter? He said: seven. Simon said: what does she like? The sailor said: I don't know. I only see her once a year."
Salma looked at the boy, her eyes shining.

"And Simon said nothing," the green boy went on. "He went behind the shelf, and brought a dried leaf from a tree in front of the store, and put it in a small envelope, and wrote on it: from Port Said. And he told him: take it to your daughter. She will understand what she likes when she sees it."
"And did his daughter like it?"

"She liked it so much that when she grew up, she came to Port Said herself. And she kept looking for the tree, until she found it. And when she was old, she sat under its shade and said: my father bought me this with a story."
And they were all quiet for a while. And then the yellow sun said in her warm voice: "That is the secret of this store, Salma. It did not sell things. It sold moments."

And at that time, her mother came and said: "Let's go, Salma, I'm done." And Salma looked at the ceiling and whispered: "A second." And her mother laughed and said: "Who are you talking to?" "The ceiling." "Okay, talk to it five more minutes."
And the green boy said: "Before your mother finishes, we want to ask you a riddle, and if you solve it we will let you take one color."
"Any color?"
"Any color you want."
And the yellow sun read the riddle:
(The answer: Simon Arzt. Game choices: Simon Arzt, the lighthouse, the war museum.)
"Simon Arzt!" said Salma. "You live in Simon's store!"
And all the colors clapped. "Bravo!"
"Choose," said the red ifrit.
Salma thought a lot. She wanted the red, and the blue, and the green, and the yellow. And in the end she said: "I want them all, but I don't have to take them. I just want to come back and see you."
The colors smiled. "That is the best choice we ever heard," said the sun. "And that is why we will give you something better."
And she put in her hand a small piece of light, like a colored spot on her palm. "Whenever you want to see us, open your hand in the sun. We will be here."
And Salma opened her hand, and saw the red and the blue and the green and the yellow dancing on her palm. And her mother came and said: "What are you doing?"
"Watching my friends."

And let me tell you something from the facts. The building has passed through many years. The sources say that many people in Port Said keep memories of the Europeans' quarter and the shops that were in it, because the city's commercial life included Greek, Italian and French communities, and each community had its churches and centers. And Port Said was a free zone before it was officially registered as such, thanks to the goods that came from the ships.

And when the building's official website spoke about its future, it said the new design will combine heritage with Art Deco, and that the glass ceiling will be reinterpreted in a new way. So even if the shape changes, the idea is the same: that this place must not lose its soul.
(Sources 1 and 4 at the end of the file.)

Salma grew up and became an interior designer. And every time she works on something new, she puts colored light into it. Her clients ask her: "Why do you love colored glass so much?" And she smiles and says: "Because people live inside it."

And one day, when she was designing a new store in Port Said, she stood in front of Simon Arzt and raised her head. The ceiling was still there. And at that moment, she heard a faint whisper: "We missed you."
And she opened her hand in the sun. And found the red bouncing on her palm, exactly as it did long ago.

And on that day, Salma brought her little daughter with her. The two stood under the ceiling, and the girl raised her head and said: "Mama, the ceiling is drawing." And Salma laughed with tears in her eyes and said: "It is not drawing, sweetheart, it is glass." And then she winked at the ceiling, and whispered: "But sometimes it draws."

[حقيقة] Simon Arzt is a big store built for sailors on the Suez Canal in Port Said. According to the official website it was built in 1922 and opened in 1923 (and the governorate says 1932), in the style of the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele, 2000 square meters, with a colored glass ceiling and wrought iron. Its owner was a tobacco farmer who arrived in Port Said in 1869 according to the website. It is currently being renovated with an Art Deco design.
[خيال] Salma, the four colors in the glass, and Simon who accepts stories instead of money: our own invention.
Your reward: the "Colors of the Glass" card (Rare, No. 008).

9.t: The Ferry: Ten Minutes Between Two Continents
9.p: Port Said and Port Fouad Ferry · Port Said
9.tz: Just ten minutes between two continents. What does someone riding the ferry hear?

secs.h: Chapter One: Two Cities and a Canal [حقيقة]
b: In Port Said, you can cross from one continent to another in less than ten minutes, and for free. This is not fiction, it is fact. Port Said is on the western bank of the canal, meaning in Africa. And Port Fouad, its twin city, is on the eastern bank, meaning in Asia. And between the two, ferries run all day, carrying people and cars, with no ticket.

And the two cities together form a transcontinental urban area, with a population of over a million people, on both banks. And Port Fouad is notable for having almost no downtown like ordinary cities, according to Wikipedia.
(Sources 1, 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Two: What Greets You in Port Fouad [حقيقة]
b: When you step off the ferry in Port Fouad, the first thing that greets you, according to a tourist guide, is the Al-Salam Mosque, which is the second mosque named Al-Salam in the two cities. And the ferries run all day, so there is no strange schedule to wait for. You arrive, you step off, you stroll, and you come back.
(Sources 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: The Boy Who Never Crossed [خيال]
b: Now let us tell a story. Once there was a boy named Mazen, seven years old. Mazen lived all his life in Port Said, but had never crossed the canal. His father was always busy, and his mother was afraid of the sea.
And one day his grandmother told him: "Come, Mazen, I will show you something."
"What?"
"I will show you how to travel from continent to continent without getting on a plane."

Mazen walked with his grandmother to the quay, and looked at the big ferry standing there. It was white and full of people: people in galabiyas, women with bags, a man holding a sheep, children running. And the sailors shouted at each other in loud voices.
"Will this take us to Asia?" asked Mazen.
"Yes."
"Do I have a passport with me?"
His grandmother laughed: "You don't need one. That is the best thing about Port Said."

Mazen got on the ferry holding his grandmother's hand. The ferry began to move slowly, the water shining, the wind hitting his face. And suddenly he felt something beautiful: that the whole world was moving with him.
"We are in the middle now," said the grandmother. "In front of you is Asia, and behind you is Africa."
Mazen looked back, and saw Port Said small, white buildings and balconies. And he looked ahead, and saw Port Fouad, green and quiet, with trees and palms.
"How many times have you crossed the canal, Granny?"
"A thousand times," said the grandmother with a smile. "Since I was little. My father used to take me with him every Friday."
"Why?"
"Because Friday was the outing day. We would go to Port Fouad, stroll, and come back."

And Mazen was busy with the people. Sitting beside him was a woman in a black scarf, holding a bag full of oranges. And in front of her a man in a leather jacket, sitting next to a big bag with something moving in it.
"What is inside the bag?" whispered Mazen to his grandmother.
"I don't know. Ask him."
"No, I'm shy."

And suddenly the bag opened, and out came the head of a big country rooster, who looked around proudly and crowed at the top of his voice: Cock-a-doodle-doo! And everyone laughed. And the man shouted as he tried to put the rooster back: "Forgive us! This rooster is spoiled by his mother!"
"This rooster crosses continents," said the woman with the oranges, laughing. "More than any of the passengers, he has a passport."

And Mazen laughed until he forgot he had been afraid. And he began looking around and noticing many people: a boy looking for his mother, a man selling biscuits, a girl looking at the water and smiling. Everyone has a story, and all of them are riding the same ferry, for the same ten minutes.
"Granny," said Mazen, "do all these people live here?"
"They are all from here," said his grandmother. "Port Said is a city that loves stories, and the ferry is the book we all read together every day."

secs.h: Chapter Five: The Man and the Sheep [خيال]
b: And in the middle of the ferry, something strange happened. The man who was holding the sheep decided to make a surprise of it. He stood on the ferry rail, raised the sheep high, and shouted: "People! Today I am crossing with a sheep from Africa to Asia! The first sheep in history!"
And the grandmother said, shaking her head: "That sheep has crossed a million times."
"How?" asked Mazen.
"At the feast, everyone brings sheep from here to there. Each sheep has crossed the canal more than the people who work at the company."

And the man kept shouting: "Where is the press? Where are the photographers?" And the people around him laughed. And someone told him: "Hagg, it's just a sheep!" And the man answered seriously: "It is an international sheep!"
And Mazen laughed until his stomach hurt.
The ferry reached Port Fouad. Mazen stepped off carefully, and put his foot on the quay. And he looked at his grandmother and said: "Am I in Asia now?"
"Yes, Mazen."
"But it looks like Port Said."
"Yes," said the grandmother. "Continents do not change the way we imagine. What changes is us."
And suddenly, he heard a voice from under the quay: "Welcome to the new visitor!"
Mazen was startled. He looked down. And inside an opening in the quay he found a small creature, wearing a sailor suit, with a cap on his head, and a big stamp in his hand.
"I am the passport officer," said the creature. "The passport officer of the continents."
"Is there a passport for Africa and Asia?" asked Mazen.
"Not an ordinary passport," said the officer. "A passport of stories. Everyone crossing the ferry for the first time must be stamped. But for me to stamp you, you must solve a riddle."
"I love riddles."
"Good. Listen:"
(The answer: the ferry. Game choices: the ferry, the lighthouse, the pedestal.)
"The ferry!" shouted Mazen.
"Bravo!" And the officer began to stamp something strange on his hand: a stamp on Mazen's palm, the shape of a small crescent and a ship. It did not hurt, and it was still warm.
The officer sat on the quay next to Mazen and his grandmother, and said: "Do you want to know who I am?"
"Yes."

"I was a real customs officer, from colonial times. I used to inspect the people crossing. And I loved my job but did not love that people felt locked in. And one day, when I saw people crossing without anyone questioning them, laughing, I decided to change my role. I became a cheerful officer, but still an officer of stamps."
"And what is the difference?"
"The difference is that people now smile when they see me."
And the grandmother laughed. "That is the best officer I have seen in my life."

And before he got up from the quay, Mazen asked the officer: "Will you stay here forever?" And the officer looked at him with fake seriousness and said: "I am the officer of the continents, my boy. My job is to welcome everyone who crosses for the first time, and also everyone who comes back after years. Each one of you will need a stamp." And then he winked: "And the stamp renews every time." And Mazen felt his hand was warm, and that the world was much wider than he had thought.
And they went back at night. The ferry was quiet, the passengers few, and the lights of Port Said shining from far away like a string of pearls. Mazen stood at the rail, his grandmother beside him.
"Granny, where are these big ships going?"
"Each one is going somewhere. That one is going to India. That one is going to Europe. And that one has not decided yet."
"And they pass from here and we cross from here. So we and the ships meet in the middle of the canal?"
"Yes," said the grandmother with a smile. "And each one says to the other in secret: safe travels."

And they were quiet, the ferry cutting through the water. And from far away, a big ship passing slowly, and on its deck a small person waving. And Mazen waved back with all his strength, knowing nobody would see him. But the ship answered with a long horn, its sound covering everything.
"It heard you!" shouted Mazen.
"Ships listen," said the grandmother. "To those who love them."

And Mazen kept waving until the ship disappeared. And then he understood that the ferry is not only a road between two banks. It is a place where people and ships and stories meet, in the middle of the canal, in the middle of the night, in the middle of the world.
And on the way back, the grandmother sat on the wooden chair next to Mazen, and looked at the water. And she said: "I know you are afraid of the sea like your mother."
"I am not afraid."
"Then why are you holding my hand so tight?"
Mazen was quiet. And then laughed. "Okay, a little."
"It's normal," said the grandmother. "I was like that. But what a person learns from the ferry is that the sea is not only water. The sea is a road. And we are the ones who learn to cross."

And Mazen held his grandmother's hand tight, and looked at the water. And noticed it was blue and gentle, and not scary. And that Port Said was coming closer to them slowly, like a grandmother opening her hand.

Mazen grew up and became a sailor. And every time he passed through the canal, he would go to the small ferry and stand in the same place where he stood with his grandmother. And look at his hand, and remember the stamp. And once he brought his daughter with him, and told her: "Come, I will show you something."
"What?"
"How to travel from continent to continent without getting on a plane."
And in the middle of the ferry, he heard the small voice again: "Welcome to the new visitor!"
And he laughed. And knew the officer was still here.

[حقيقة] The Port Said and Port Fouad ferries are free, run all day, the trip takes under ten minutes, and they carry people and cars. Port Said is in Africa and Port Fouad is in Asia, and the two cities together have over a million residents. In Port Fouad the Al-Salam Mosque greets those who step off the ferry, according to a tourist guide.
[خيال] Mazen, his grandmother, the man and the sheep, and the passport officer of the continents: our own invention.
Your reward: the "Officer of the Continents" card (Rare, No. 009).

10.t: Lady of the Balcony: She Who Knows the Old Street Names
10.p: Al-Afrang Quarter, Al-Tigara Street (now Al-Nahda) · Port Said
10.tz: The Lady of the Balcony has sat there for ages. She knows the old street names, but she will tell you on one condition.

secs.h: Chapter One: A City of Balconies [حقيقة]
b: If you walk into old downtown Port Said and look up, you will find something missing in many Egyptian cities: balconies. Big balconies on every floor, many of them wooden, wide verandas that give the city its special look. They say these buildings were three to four floors, with facades marked by wooden verandas.

The reason is that Port Said was built in a special way. The city had no resources: no stone, no wood, nothing. Everything was brought from outside. And the first houses came ready-made in crates, and were mostly built of wood.
(Sources 1 and 2 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Two: A City of Every Nationality [حقيقة]
b: And the people living in these houses came from everywhere. The sources say Port Said was a cosmopolitan city from the day it was built, and that it flourished especially in the nineteenth century and the first half of the twentieth. People of different nationalities and religions lived there, mostly from Mediterranean countries, and lived together in tolerance.

And a Port Said historian named Diaa Eldin El-Kady says that in the early fifties, before 56, it was normal to see Italians, Greeks and French in the cafes, markets and cinemas, and each community had its churches and centers. The most famous quarter was Al-Afrang quarter, and it had about 15 different nationalities.
And one of its most important commercial streets was "Al-Tigara Street", whose name is now Al-Nahda Street. It had about 300 Greek shops, among them well-known ones like Baudoin, Selecta and Mikado.
(Source 3 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: The Girl Who Looked Up [خيال]
b: And in this quarter, in an old building with a round wooden balcony, there was a girl named Nour, ten years old. Nour loved to walk the streets and look up. And every time she passed along Al-Nahda Street, she stopped in front of one particular building and looked at a balcony on the second floor.
Because on that balcony sat a woman. An older woman, in an old dress with roses, with white hair, and a tea glass in her hand. And she looked down at the passersby, and smiled.
One day, Nour found the courage. She stood under the balcony and said: "Good morning!"
"Good morning, light," answered the woman from above in a gentle voice. "What is your name?"
"Nour."
"A lovely name. And I am the Lady of the Balcony."
"The Lady of the Balcony?" laughed Nour. "Is that your real name?"
"The only name I remember," said the woman. "Those who passed here years ago no longer remember my name. But they still remember the balcony."
"And have you lived here a long time?"

"Since before you were born, and before your father was born. From the days when this street was called Al-Tigara Street, and had 300 Greek shops, and people spoke three languages in the same sentence."
Nour stood with her mouth open. "You saw that?"
"I saw everything," said the woman. "From here the whole world shows."
"Can I come up?"
"No, my dear. Whoever comes and stands below must answer my questions first. I am a lady of questions."
And the lady said: "The first question: there were many nationalities in this quarter. Can you tell me how many?"
Nour thought. "I don't know. But I heard my grandfather say something about fifteen."

"Bravo!" the lady clapped. "About fifteen nationalities. Greeks and Italians and French and others, and each community had its churches and centers. And they lived side by side. And I saw all of them from above."
"And how did they talk?"
"In every way. With gestures, with jokes, with food. That is what I learned from them: that language is no problem if people want to understand."
Nour smiled. And said: "The second question?"

secs.h: Chapter Six: Baudoin, Selecta and Mikado [خيال]
b: "The second question," said the lady as she put the glass on the balcony rail, "the names of three shops that were here. And if you know them, I will tell you the story of each one."
"Baudoin... and Selecta... and Mikado!" said Nour quickly. "My grandfather told me!"
"Bravo, bravo!" the lady clapped with trembling hands. "Now that is a memory. Come, listen."

And the lady told, her voice changing with each story. About a shop where all the children stood in front of its window every feast, because it had toys that moved. And about another shop whose owner was a huge Greek man who wore a red tie, and loved to laugh with customers, and gave every child a sweet. And about a third shop with shelves full of things from every country, and each thing came with a small card saying where it came from.
[خيال] And all these stories are our own invention, but they try to tell the feeling of the street, not its details.
And suddenly, they heard a voice coming from the balcony opposite, from the building on the other side of the street. "Fatma! Are you telling stories to a little girl again?"
And Nour looked, and found another woman, in a purple dress, holding a paper fan, looking at them with a defiant look.
"That is the Lady of the Window," whispered the Lady of the Balcony. "My neighbor for ages. And she has been fighting with me since about 1930."
"Over what?"
"Over which of us has the nicest balcony."
And the Lady of the Window shouted from far away: "Your balcony is old, Fatma! Mine is more modern!"
"Yours is not round!" answered the Lady of the Balcony defiantly. "And the round one is the original!"

And Nour laughed, thinking this was the longest fight she had ever heard in her life, and that it was done with obvious love. And the Lady of the Window began to lower a small basket on a rope, with a glass of tea and a piece of kahk in it. And she said: "This is for the girl who listens. Not for you, Fatma."
"You don't love me?" asked the Lady of the Balcony in annoyance.
"I love you more than anyone," said the Lady of the Window. "But I won't admit it."
And the two women laughed out loud, and Nour laughed with them. And understood that in old neighborhoods, even fights are a form of love.

secs.h: Chapter Six (prelude): Those Who Left and Those Who Stayed [حقيقة وخيال]
b: [حقيقة] The sources say foreign communities led commercial activity in Port Said from the twenties until the fifties, that the Greek community dominated retail trade, and that it built big warehouses in the city from which goods were distributed to Egyptian cities. And the changes that came afterward changed the look of the quarter.

[خيال] "Everyone who left left something behind," said the Lady of the Balcony quietly. "One left a key, one left a notebook, and one woman left me a rose in a pot. And I kept all of it, so that if they came back, they would find their things."
"And did they come back?"
"Some," she said. "After years. They came to visit Port Said, and stood under the balcony and looked up. And I said nothing. But I threw them a rose."
"The third and last question," said the lady, "is a riddle."
(The answer: Al-Nahda Street. Game choices: Al-Nahda Street, Al-Horreya Street, Al-Gomhuriya Street.)
"Al-Nahda Street!" said Nour quickly.
"Correct!" shouted the Lady of the Balcony, laughing. "It was called Al-Tigara Street, and people still remember. I am happy."
"Come," said the lady. "Come up."
"But you said I would not come up!"
"I said if you did not answer. You answered."

And at that moment, something strange happened. A small wooden staircase appeared from the balcony, coming down to the pavement, without anyone knowing where it came from. And Nour climbed carefully, the wood making a sweet creaking sound. And finally, she reached the balcony.

It was the loveliest thing she had ever seen. She could see the whole street from above: the shops, the people, the other balconies. And every balcony in the street had a light, and on every balcony someone sat. A woman and a man and a boy and a girl, and all of them waving to each other.
"Who are they?" asked Nour.
"My neighbors," said the lady. "Every balcony has someone, but only the one who climbs up here can see them."

Nour sat on a chair next to the lady. They drank tea, and talked. Nour told about her school and her friends and her dreams. And the lady told about many people who came and went: Greeks who went back to their countries, Italians who traveled, and the people of Port Said who stayed. And in every story she smiled a little sadly.
"Why are you sad?" asked Nour.
"I am not sad," said the lady. "I am just remembering. And I miss many people."
"And will you stay here?"
"As long as someone passes in the street and looks up," said the lady. "You looked. So I am here."

Nour grew up. And became a photographer. And she loved photographing balconies. And she had a famous photo, a photo of a round wooden balcony, with an empty chair and a tea glass on the rail. And people would ask: "Where is the lady?"
And she would answer: "She is there, but not everyone sees her."
And one day, while she was photographing on Al-Nahda Street, a little boy stood next to her and said: "What are you photographing?"
"A balcony."
"Is there someone in it?"
Nour smiled. "There is a lady. Her name is the Lady of the Balcony. If you answer three questions, you will go up and sit with her."

[حقيقة] Port Said was built on land with no resources, and its early houses were brought ready-made and mostly of wood. The Europeans' quarter had about 15 nationalities, and Al-Tigara Street (now Al-Nahda) had about 300 Greek shops including Baudoin, Selecta and Mikado, according to the historian Diaa Eldin El-Kady. The big balconies on every floor are an architectural mark of the city.
[خيال] Nour, the Lady of the Balcony, the wooden stairs, her three questions, and the stories of the shops: all our own invention.
Your reward: the "Lady of the Balcony" card (Rare, No. 010).

11.t: The Military Museum: The Story You Cannot Make Up
11.p: Port Said Military Museum, 23 July Street · Port Said
11.tz: Inside the Military Museum the story is not made up. But there is a question that will make you look again.

secs.h: Chapter One: Why Port Said Has a Military Museum [حقيقة]
b: In Port Said on 23 July Street, in front of a military hospital, there is a museum on about seven thousand square meters. It is called the Port Said Military Museum. And this museum is not only a weapons museum, it is a city museum.

The Ministry of Defense website itself says the museum was founded in 1964 to commemorate the Tripartite Aggression on Port Said in 1956, and that it is a witness to the heroism of the people of Port Said in defending their land. And some sources say the idea of the museum began in 1963 and that its location was a garden called Bint El-Nil Garden.

And the date it opened was not by chance. It opened on December 23, 1964, which is Port Said's National Day, the day the last soldier of the aggressing forces withdrew from the city in 1956. So the museum opened on the same day the city celebrates.
(Sources 1, 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Two: What Is Inside the Walls [حقيقة]
b: The museum has been renovated more than once. In 1978 a hall was added for October War artifacts, and it was opened then by Prime Minister Mamdouh Salem according to Wikipedia. And then it was renovated and reopened on December 23, 2009.

And according to the archaeologist Sameh El-Zahar in a statement to the Middle East News Agency, the museum has four halls: the main lobby that tells about the ancient era, the Suez Canal hall, the Tripartite Aggression hall, and the October 1973 hall. It also has an open display yard.

And the Ministry of Defense website mentions in the open yard heavy equipment and reconnaissance aircraft that were captured or used in the 1956 and 1973 wars, and mentions models depicting battles like the Battle of Al-Gamil, the Battle of Al-Manakh quarter, and the Battle of Ras El-Esh, and also models of the digging of the Suez Canal and its opening.
(Sources 1, 4 and 5 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: What You Hear When You Walk Slowly [خيال]
b: And now the made-up part, and it is not about a battle, it is about a visit.

One December day, an old man named Uncle Salah walked in the garden, with his grandson Youssef, nine years old. Uncle Salah took part in no war, he was just a child in the fifties, and he has small memories, not heroics: the sound of a siren, his mother pulling him by the hand, people running.
Youssef asked: "Grandpa, do these tanks move?"
"No, my dear. They are standing. But they are not silent."
"How are they not silent?"
The man smiled and said: "Walk with me, and you will hear."

They went in through the lobby. And in the Suez Canal hall, they stood in front of the works telling the story of the canal. The official website says this hall has artworks about the story of the canal and documents.
Youssef stood in front of the canal digging model and asked: "Did they dig it by hand?"

And here Uncle Salah said something real, from written history: that the canal was dug by the labor of a great many people, and that the company that ran the canal was foreign until it was nationalized in 1956. And that is exactly the point where the museum's story begins: when President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal Company on July 26, 1956.
(Source 3 at the end of the file, and this is an account from a tourism website and it agrees with the well-known account.)
And then they went into the Tripartite Aggression hall. The sources say it is the heart of the museum.

The short story, as it is written: Britain and France, in cooperation with Israel, responded to the nationalization of the canal with a military operation. British and French forces landed in and around Port Said in November 1956. They were resisted by Egyptian soldiers and civilian volunteers. The city was shelled and damaged, and civilians died. And after international pressure, the forces withdrew within weeks, and the last withdrawal was on December 23. From here the city took its National Day.
The hall displays photos, maps, weapons, uniforms, models, newspapers and captured equipment. And among the names of areas remembered in the models: Al-Gamil, Al-Manakh quarter and Ras El-Esh.
(Sources 1, 3 and 4 at the end of the file. The museum is an official Egyptian account and we relay it as it is without adding details to it.)

secs.h: Chapter Six: Youssef Asks the Hard Question [خيال]
b: Youssef stood in front of one of the models, and watched the small figures in it. And then he asked: "Were they afraid?"

Uncle Salah was quiet for a while. He had no answer from the sources, and did not want to invent heroics in the mouth of someone who died. And finally he said: "I don't know, Youssef. And I should not tell you something I don't know. What I know is that what happened happened to real people, and that they lived in the streets you are walking in."
"So we don't say they were not afraid?"
"I say they were people. And that is enough."
And Youssef was quiet, and then took his grandfather's hand, and they moved on.

They went out to the yard. They stood in front of an American Patton tank, which the Ministry website says was used in the October 1973 war. And there is a light reconnaissance helicopter, and an Israeli 155 mm howitzer. All of them are listed in the photo gallery on the Ministry website.
And there is a statue called "Egypt Through the Ages" and a statue "The Egyptian Soldier" in the lobby, according to the same website.

A tourism website that visited the museum says the usual visit lasts between half an hour and forty five minutes, and that the museum's tone is official, patriotic and direct. This is not a museum that shows all sides at the same distance, it is a museum of memory. And it is important to know this when you enter.
(Sources 4 and 6 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Eight: The One That Is Not Silent [خيال]
b: Youssef stood in front of the tank and put his hand on the iron, which was warm from the sun. And he said: "Grandpa, I heard."
"You heard what?"
"The tank is saying something."
"What is it saying?"
Youssef thought. "Not words. It just says: remember."
Uncle Salah smiled, and said nothing. Because he understood. This museum does not fight, it remembers. And everyone who enters leaves carrying a piece of the memory, even if they were not alive then.
And he took a small paper from his pocket, and wrote today's date on it, and held Youssef's hand and said: "We will bring your mother with us next time."

And let me tell you, as the narrator, what must be said openly. All the dates in this story are from sources: 1964 for the opening, 2009 for the reopening, December 23 for the National Day. But the story of Uncle Salah and Youssef is not real, and we meant it that way. We did not want to put in the mouth of any real person who lived or died words they did not say.
And if you are a visitor, remember that in this museum real people are remembered, and that you are coming to look at a place that presents a city's account of itself.
The riddle: I was opened on a feast day, not on an ordinary day. I opened the day the strangers left. I do not fight, but I remember. Who am I?
The choices in the game:
1. The Military Museum
2. The lighthouse
3. The train station
The answer: the Military Museum. It opened on December 23, 1964, Port Said's National Day.

[حقيقة] The museum opened on December 23, 1964 to commemorate the 1956 Tripartite Aggression, on about 7000 square meters. The October hall was added in 1978 and it was renovated and reopened on December 23, 2009. It has the Suez Canal, Tripartite Aggression and October halls, and an open yard with equipment and models.
[خيال] Uncle Salah and Youssef and the dialogue between them: our own invention, and they include no real person.
Your reward: the "Remember" card (Rare, No. 011).

12.t: The Fishermen of Manzala: The Net That Catches Stories
12.p: Lake Manzala, Al-Qabouti Area and the Connecting Canal · Port Said
12.tz: The fishermen on Lake Manzala cast their net. This time it caught a story.

secs.h: Chapter One: A Lake Bigger Than a City [حقيقة]
b: If you head south out of Port Said, you will find a lot of water that is not the sea and not the canal. This is Lake Manzala. And Wikipedia says it is one of the largest and most fertile natural lakes in Egypt.

It connects to the Suez Canal near southern Port Said through a passage called the "Connecting Canal". And it connects to the Mediterranean through openings called the "boghaz", among them Boghaz El-Gamil. These boghaz are how fish go in and out, and they keep the water from being stagnant.

The numbers about its size vary: before the filling and drying, its area was about 750 thousand feddans, meaning 50 kilometers long and 30 to 35 kilometers wide, which is about a tenth of the whole Delta. And then the area fell to about 190 thousand feddans in 1990, and about 125 thousand feddans today, according to the same article.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

And at one time, the lake produced about 48% of Egypt's natural lake production, according to Wikipedia. That means about half the fish that came from the lakes came from here. The reason is that the natural food is plentiful, the weather is mild most of the year, and the sea is near.
And there is an old picture, a drawing of a fishing boat on Manzala, from 1878. So fishing there is not new, it has hundreds of pictures and stories.

But the lake has gone through problems. Wikipedia mentions environmental problems, like garbage, pollution from drains, blocked boghaz and factory waste, and security problems because of thugs. And all this affected the fishermen.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: Uncle Abdo and His Little Passenger [خيال]
b: Back to the story. One winter day, there was a fisherman named Uncle Abdo, with a small boat named "Umm El-Kheir", and a grandson named Karim, ten years old, who came with him every Friday.
And Uncle Abdo had a strange habit. Every time he cast the net, he said in a low voice: "Give me what you have, lake. Fish or story, I don't care."
And Karim would laugh. "Grandpa, the net only catches fish."
"You are still young, Karim," Uncle Abdo would say, pulling the rope. "The net catches whatever wants to be caught."

secs.h: Chapter Four: What Came Up in the Net [خيال]
b: That Friday, the net got heavy. So heavy that Uncle Abdo and Karim pulled it together, counting to three, then two, then one.
The net came up, and they found in it tilapia and catfish and small coral. And they found something strange too: a book. A wet book, with a green cover, without one dry page.
"Is that a book?" asked Karim.

"It is something bigger than a book," said Uncle Abdo, opening it gently. And on the first page, there was ink still moving, like a small fish swimming. And the ink wrote letters, and then words: "My name is Boghaz. I am the one between the lake and the sea."
"His name is Boghaz!" whispered Karim. "Like Boghaz El-Gamil!"

The book opened itself page by page. And on every page there was a story that changed each time. Once about a fish that wanted to see the sea, so she followed the water to the boghaz. Once about a boat lost in the fog that kept circling for three days. Once about a fisherman who met an old woman on the shore who asked him: "Why do you catch so much?"
And Boghaz told, and the fishermen nearby heard the voice and came to watch from their boats. And they stood silent, each with his net in his hand, listening.
"This book is told," said Uncle Abdo. "Not read."

secs.h: Chapter Six: The Truth Gets On the Boat [حقيقة]
b: And here let me go back to the sources a little. Al-Watan newspaper published in 2012 a report about the fishermen of Al-Qabouti area in Port Said. Al-Qabouti is on the Connecting Canal between the lake and the Suez Canal, according to the same report. And the area's residents said then that they suffered from lawlessness, and from a chemical factory next to them they say affected the water and fish.

And then in 2022, Cairo24 website quoted the governor of Port Said saying that the cleaning operations within the governorate were completed 100%, and that about 18 thousand feddans of reeds and weeds were removed, and that fishermen say the water became cleaner and new kinds of fish appeared.
And this is press reporting, not a scientific study. So it is a picture of the fishermen's situation as relayed, not a final judgment.
(Sources 2, 3 and 4 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Seven: What Happens When the Net Wears Out [خيال]
b: Back to the boat. Over time, Boghaz began to tell sad stories. A story about water that became heavy. A story about a fish that never came back. A story about a fisherman forced to leave the lake and go somewhere else.
All the fishermen fell silent. And Karim tugged his grandfather's sleeve and said: "Grandpa, is it crying?"
"No, Karim. It is remembering."
And then the page turned, and Boghaz began to tell a new story. About a clean shore. About a net that came up full. About a small boy laughing while holding a fish bigger than his hand.
"It is dreaming," said Karim.
"All fishermen dream," said Uncle Abdo. "That is half the job."
When the sun was about to set, the book of Boghaz closed itself. And they heard its voice one last time: "I cannot stay with you. I must go back to the sea. But I will leave you something."
And in Karim's hand, a small dry paper appeared. On it was only one word: "Ask."
"Is that all?" said Karim.
"That is a lot," said Uncle Abdo. "Whoever asks, knows. And whoever does not ask only catches fish."
And the man threw the book into the water with his own hand, and it vanished among the waves.

And after that, every Friday, Karim asked his grandfather one question. Once: "Where does the water come from?" And once: "Why do the fish run away?" And once: "What makes the net heavy?" And Uncle Abdo would answer if he knew, and if he did not know he would say: "We will ask someone who knows."

secs.h: Chapter Nine: A Page from the Truth [حقيقة]
b: And let me tell you something important as the narrator. This story does not say everything is fine. Port Said's own press says the fishermen had real problems: illegal fishing, licenses, electric fishing, and boat sizes, according to an Al-Watan report in 2019 about the crises of Manzala fishermen. And these are things a story cannot solve.

What we did was take a real place, and real people who work in it, and put inside it a grandson and a book that tells. But the grandson and the book are not real. And the real fishermen deserve more appreciation than any story.
(Source 5 at the end of the file.)
The riddle: I am not a sea and not a river. A fish enters me from a small opening and leaves from it. My name resembles the name of an area in Port Said. Who am I?
The choices in the game:
1. Lake Manzala
2. Lake Timsah
3. Lake Qarun
The answer: Lake Manzala. Its area used to be about 750 thousand feddans, and it connects to the sea through the boghaz.

[حقيقة] Manzala is one of Egypt's largest natural lakes, its area fell from about 750 thousand feddans to about 125 thousand. It connects to the Suez Canal through the "Connecting Canal" near Port Said, and to the sea through the boghaz. It used to produce about 48% of the natural lakes' production. It suffered from environmental and security problems, and fishermen say the cleaning improved the water.
[خيال] Uncle Abdo, Karim, and the telling book of Boghaz: our own invention.

13.t: The Train Station: The Horse That Never Arrives
13.p: Port Said Railway Station, 15 May Square · Port Said
13.tz: The old train station, and a horse that never arrives. Where is it headed?

secs.h: Chapter One: The Train Before the Building [حقيقة]
b: The train reached Port Said years before the station we see today. The sources say Khedive Abbas Hilmi II opened the first railway line linking Port Said to Ismailia on December 3, 1893. Then in 1904 the Cairo to Ismailia line was extended to Port Said.

So more than a hundred years ago, people were boarding in Cairo and getting off in Port Said, and goods were moving on rails instead of boats. And the station is the end point. The train that arrives here does not continue, because after Port Said there is sea.
(Sources 1 and 2 at the end of the file.)

The building standing today was built in 1955 at a cost of 220 thousand pounds, and opened in the early sixties, according to Al-Balad newspaper and Wikipedia. It is located in 15 May Square in the East quarter.

And in 2017, the station manager told Al-Ahram newspaper that development and restoration work was underway, and that the first phase includes the main hall, the clock tower, the offices and the departure and arrival halls, and that the cost passed 80 million pounds, preserving the historic character. And a contracting company published that the project ran from 2016 to 2020.
And there is a small difference between sources on the number of platforms: Wikipedia says 8, and the company says 6. So we will not put a number.
(Sources 2, 3, 4 and 5 at the end of the file.)

Back to the story. There is a boy named Walid, eight years old, and every Tuesday he goes with his father to the train station, because his uncle comes from Cairo by train and brings him a small something every time.

Walid loved to sit on the bench in the hall and look at the big murals. And in one of them there was a horse pulling a heavy cart. This horse in particular drew him, because its muscles stood out, as if it would move at any moment.
And one day, the train an hour late, and his father drinking tea, Walid looked at the horse and found it looking at him.

secs.h: Chapter Four: Who Painted the Horse [حقيقة]
b: And before we go on with the story, I want to tell you who really painted this horse.

In the station's main hall there are two heritage murals, each measuring 27 meters by 6 meters, according to Al-Balad newspaper. The one on the right as you enter was painted by the artist Abdel Aziz Khaled Darwish (1918 to 1981). It depicts the history of land transport: simple carts pulled by horses and animals, and the horse's muscles stand out as he pulls a heavy load, and also cars and trains and telegraph and telephone poles. And the source says the painting was done in the sixties, at the same time as the station's opening.
And this artist received a professorship in painting from the San Fernando Academy in Madrid in 1952.

And the one on the left was painted by the artist Hosni Mohamed El-Banani (1912 to 1988), and it depicts sea and air transport: small boats and sailing boats and big ships, and a blue sky with planes.
(Source 3 at the end of the file.)
"Aren't you going with them?" the horse said to Walid, in a voice like iron on iron.
Walid was not startled. He is the kind of boy who believes. "Going where?"
"The train. Every day it comes, and it leaves. And I have stood here since the day I was painted, pulling this cart, and I have never arrived."
"Why?"
"Because whoever painted me did not paint a place for me to go. He painted me a road only."
And the horse was quiet a bit, and then said: "Every day I see people come and people leave. And I count. Do you know how many trains I have counted?"
"How many?"
"I don't know. I forget the number every time. But I have never forgotten a single face."

secs.h: Chapter Six: A Trip Inside the Mural [خيال]
b: And in a moment, the horse pulled Walid by the hand, and Walid was inside the mural. And here old cars were passing beside him, a tall telegraph pole, and a small train puffing smoke.
"Is that it?" asked Walid.
"That is the first train," said the horse. "The one that reached Port Said for the first time."

And Walid boarded it, and found himself in a wooden car, with a window in front of him. And from the window, he saw the desert and the sea and the canal. And he saw people in tarbooshes and hats, and little girls with dolls.
And Walid said: "I don't want to go back."
"You must," said the horse quietly. "Your father will worry."
Before they went back, the horse stopped in front of a strange door. Behind it was the sea.
"This is the second mural," he said. "The one on the left. This one is of the sea and the sky."
And Walid saw white boats with sails, and big ships rising in the waves, and little planes in the blue sky.
"Why don't you go there?" he asked.
"Because that is not my place." The horse smiled. "I am a land horse. But I watch my friends from afar."
And on the boats of the second mural there was a small boat with a name written on it. Walid looked, and found it said "Walid". And he laughed. "That is me!"
"Of course," said the horse. "Every boy who comes here finds a boat with his name."
And he opened his eyes, and found himself on the bench. And his father in front of him, shaking his shoulder: "Walid! The train arrived!"
And his uncle came, carrying a small bag. And said: "I brought you something."
And Walid found in the bag a small wooden horse. Pulling a wooden cart.
"Thank you, Uncle," said Walid, his heart pounding. And he looked at the mural. The horse in it stood as it was.
But Walid saw, and he is sure, that the horse winked at him.

And let me tell you the part from reality. The station really has two murals, and one really has a horse pulling a heavy load, and one has ships and planes. That is according to the source that wrote about the artists. But what we do not know is whether the source describes every detail as it is today after the restoration, so someone needs to go and see with their own eyes.
And in the story, Walid and the talking horse and the trip inside the mural are all fiction.
And in reality, the Port Said station is one of the city's landmarks, according to the local press. And every train that arrives is the end of one journey, and the start of another.
The riddle: I am a beginning for some people and an end for others. The train that enters me does not continue. In my hall there are two big paintings: one for land and one for sea. Who am I?
The choices in the game:
1. Port Said Railway Station
2. Port Said Port
3. The lighthouse
The answer: Port Said Railway Station. And it has two murals, on the right for land transport and on the left for sea and air.

[حقيقة] The first railway line between Port Said and Ismailia opened on December 3, 1893, and the Cairo line was extended in 1904. The current building was built in 1955 for 220 thousand pounds and opened in the early sixties. It has two murals of 27 by 6 meters: by Abdel Aziz Darwish (land) and by Hosni El-Banani (sea and air). The station was renovated from 2016 to 2020.
[خيال] Walid, the talking horse and the trip inside the mural: our own invention.
Your reward: the "Horse That Pulls" card (Rare, No. 013).

14.t: Al-Salam Mosque: The Dove Who Delivers Greetings
14.p: Al-Salam Mosque and the Garden Beside It, Atef Sadat and Al-Gomhuriya Street, East District · Port Said
14.tz: In the garden next to Al-Salam Mosque there is a dove that is not ordinary. What does she deliver?

secs.h: Chapter One: A Mosque Overlooking Two Seas [حقيقة]
b: In the East district, at the intersection of Atef Sadat and Al-Gomhuriya streets, there is a mosque called Al-Salam Mosque. Its area is about 1100 meters, and it was built in 1992, according to Al-Youm Al-Sabea newspaper.

It is not the oldest mosque in Port Said, because the Tawfiqi Mosque is much older. But Al-Salam Mosque has an advantage in location: it is at the northeastern entrance of the city, and overlooks the Suez Canal's shipping channel and the Mediterranean. So whoever stands beside it sees water from more than one side.
And the source says that although it is modern, it became a destination for locals who come to Port Said from other governorates, and also for foreign delegations.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Two: What Is Inside and Around It [حقيقة]
b: The mosque has a large prayer hall for men and a small annex, a prayer hall for women, a big garden surrounding it on the west side, and halls for occasions like marriage contracts. And next to the mosque is a big garden with benches for the locals, and many events are held in it.
And in Ramadan it holds lessons of knowledge and Taraweeh and Tahajjud prayers.

And every year, on Port Said's National Day on December 23, which is the anniversary of the evacuation after the Tripartite Aggression, the mosque usually hosts the Minister of Endowments and the Mufti, and the sermon is broadcast from it on Egyptian television, according to the same source.
And in an article about the ferry between Port Said and Port Fouad, a tourist guide says Al-Salam Mosque is among the first landmarks seen by someone getting off the ferry in Port Said.
(Sources 1 and 2 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: Mariam Waits for the Ferry [خيال]
b: Back to the story. One winter day in Port Said, there was a girl named Mariam, nine years old, living in Port Fouad and going to school in Port Said every day by ferry. And with her was her little brother Ziad, five years old, holding her hand gently.
Every day, when the ferry got close, Mariam would look at the minaret of Al-Salam Mosque appearing from afar. And say to Ziad: "See? That is Al-Salam. It means we have arrived."
And Ziad would ask the same question every day: "Why is Al-Salam called that?"
And every day Mariam would answer: "Because it greets us."
And Mariam was not sure of that answer. But she felt it was right.
And on Wednesday, the ferry was late, and they came out earlier than the usual time. So Mariam said to Ziad: "Let's sit in the garden a while."
And they sat on a bench next to the mosque. And beside them a white dove, looking tired, walking on the ground as if searching for something.
"Is she lost?" asked Ziad.
"I don't think so," said Mariam. "She is working."
The dove stopped and looked at them, and said in a clear voice: "Indeed. I am working."
Ziad opened his mouth and closed it. Mariam, who was always confident, said: "You talk?"
"Of course. My name is Sabah. I am a mail carrier." And she spread her wing a bit. "But not ordinary mail. I deliver greetings."
"How do you deliver greetings?" asked Mariam, and sat on the ground beside her.

"Simple," said Sabah. "People come here and say 'peace be upon you' to each other. And I listen. And then I take the greeting and deliver it to anyone who needs it. The ships passing in the canal, the sailors far from their families, the people in Port Fouad watching us from afar."
"And do they hear?"
"Not with the ear. With the heart." And Sabah tilted her head back. "Every time someone says a greeting sincerely, it turns into a small white feather. And I take it and fly with it."
And she pulled from under her wing a very small white feather. "This one has not been delivered yet. To whom?"
"To us?" asked Ziad.
"To you," said Sabah. "Every day you cross and tell yourselves that the mosque greets you. I heard. And that is the loveliest greeting I have heard in a while."
And at that moment, they heard a ship's horn. Far, but clear. And Sabah raised her head.
"That is a ship from far away. Her name is 'Maria'. On board is a sailor named Yannis. He needs someone to tell him he has arrived in Egypt. But he does not speak Arabic."
"I know how to say hello in English!" said Ziad excitedly.
"We don't need a language," said Sabah. "We need intention."
And then she said to Mariam: "Say hello to him. Loud, in your voice. And I will deliver it."
And Mariam stood on the bench, looked toward the canal, and said in a loud voice: "Welcome to Egypt!" And then, because Ziad pulled her dress, she also said: "Peace be upon you!"
A small white feather appeared in the air, and Sabah caught it in her beak, and flew toward the canal.
After a minute, Sabah came back. And in her beak was a small paper. She handed it to Mariam.
On it was a pencil drawing: the face of a laughing man, in a sailor's cap, his hand raised. And beneath it one word: "Thanks".
"Is that him?" asked Ziad.
"That is Yannis," said Sabah. "He loved the greeting. And he sent you this."
And Mariam laughed, and put the drawing in her notebook. "It will stay with me."
"And will you bring me another greeting?" asked Ziad.
"Every day God willing," said Sabah. "As long as there are people who give greetings."

secs.h: Chapter Eight: When the Truth Enters the Story [حقيقة]
b: And let me go back to reality. The mosque is relatively modern, and it is important to say so openly: it is not one of the old monuments. But the age of a place does not always decide its value. And the article we relied on says it became part of the city's official celebrations, because the National Day sermon is broadcast from it.

Also, and this is from a tourist guide, Port Said and Port Fouad are twins on the two banks of the canal. Port Said is on the African bank and Port Fouad on the Asian, and between them are free ferries all day, and the crossing takes under 10 minutes. And that is the basis on which we built the story of Mariam and Ziad.
But Mariam and Ziad and Sabah and Yannis and the ship "Maria" are not real.
(Sources 1, 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Nine: The Garden at Night [خيال]
b: And in the evening, when the sun went down behind the mosque, the garden quieted. The children left, and the chairs emptied. And Sabah went back to her garden, and sat in a nearby tree.

And around her, small white feathers began to glow in the dark. Each feather a greeting said today. One from an old man who met his friend after years. One from a child who greeted the teacher. One from a bride and groom leaving the event hall with people congratulating them.
"All these greetings must be delivered," Sabah told herself, and gathered the feathers gently, and flew.
And in the morning, when Mariam and Ziad came to the ferry, they saw on the garden wall a small white feather. And Mariam reached out, and put it inside her notebook beside Yannis's drawing.
"Does this one want to be delivered?" asked Ziad.
"No," said Mariam. "This one is for us."

The riddle: I am not the oldest mosque in the city, but I am the first thing seen by someone getting off the ferry. I overlook a canal and a sea together. And a sermon is broadcast from me on the city's feast day. Who am I?
The choices in the game:
1. Al-Salam Mosque
2. Al-Abbasi Mosque
3. Al-Tawfiqi Mosque
The answer: Al-Salam Mosque. It was built in 1992 and overlooks the canal and the Mediterranean.

[حقيقة] Al-Salam Mosque was built in 1992 on about 1100 meters in the East district (Atef Sadat and Al-Gomhuriya street), at the northeastern entrance of the city, overlooking the canal and the Mediterranean. It has a men's and women's prayer hall, a garden and event halls. The National Day sermon (December 23) is usually broadcast from it.
[خيال] Mariam, Ziad, the dove Sabah, the greeting feathers and the sailor Yannis: our own invention.
Your reward: the "Dove Sabah" card (Common, No. 014).

15.t: The Corniche: The Black Flag and Cabin Number Seven
15.p: Port Said Corniche and Beach · Port Said
15.tz: A black flag and cabin number seven on the beach. What is their secret?

secs.h: Chapter One: A City Without a Beach [حقيقة]
b: Today the Corniche in Port Said is taken for granted. A sea, a beach and people walking. But an article in Sada Al-Balad says something strange: that Port Said had almost no bathing beaches until the early twentieth century.

The reason is that the northern shore had a lot of sand, and the northwest winds brought it onto the city. So much that the municipal council built barriers in front of the sand so it would not enter the city. And then they moved the sand to the west side and used it to fill parts of Lake Manzala.

And in the early twentieth century, the Suez Canal Company built a modest resort for its workers and employees on the other bank, before Port Fouad opened on December 21, 1926. It consisted of simple wooden cabins.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

And this article says something else strange: that the beach was dangerous at first, because sharks multiplied after the Port Said slaughterhouse was built, and the remains of the slaughtered animals were thrown into the canal directly.

So before anyone thought of swimming, the city had to deal with a slaughterhouse problem. A funny and strange story, and it is in the article as it is, and we do not confirm its details from another source.

And in 1911 the Port Said municipal council appeared, and began to think about the beach. It announced that it would lease beach land to anyone who wanted to build a wooden bathhouse for summering, at an annual rent of 3 and a half pounds.

And in the council session on July 2, 1913, a member named Monsieur Metrovitch complained that the roads leading to the main street were neglected and full of dust, that the free water tap had been replaced with a tap selling water, and that there were no trash bins. And the council chairman replied that he would order maintenance.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: Uncle Sobhi and Cabin Seven [خيال]
b: Back to the story. One summer, there was a man named Uncle Sobhi, who had a small wooden bathhouse on the shore, number seven. Something simple: a room the size of a big wardrobe, with a nail for hanging clothes and a small mirror.

Uncle Sobhi thought himself the most important man in Port Said, because he was in charge of the cabin where everyone changed. And he had a habit of asking every customer: "Is the sea nice today?" And everyone answered. And when someone did not answer, he would say: "He hasn't seen the sea yet."
And one day, a boy named Sami, eight years old, came to change his clothes. He went into the cabin, closed the door, opened the door after a minute, and said: "Uncle Sobhi, there is someone inside."
"What?" said Uncle Sobhi, and looked inside.
There was a very small man, exactly one span tall, in a black suit and a tarboosh, sitting on the nail.
"Who are you, sir?" said Uncle Sobhi, without being startled. He is a man who has seen a lot in his life.
"I am the Black Flag," said the small man in a serious voice. "I am the one who is hung when the sea is angry."
"And what are you doing in my cabin?"
"Hiding. The black flag is hung once a day, and the rest of the day I have no work. So I sit in places with the nicest mirror."
And he looked at himself in the small mirror, and adjusted the tarboosh. "This mirror is good."

secs.h: Chapter Five: What Was Forbidden on the Beach [حقيقة]
b: And here I must tell you something real, and you will laugh. In 1949, the municipal council issued a decision organizing the bathing beach with 22 articles. And among what was forbidden, according to the Sada Al-Balad article:

Setting up kiosks or umbrellas or tents without a permit. Using the cabins to sleep in or stay in after sunset. Going into the sea while the black flag is raised. Fishing along the beach designated for bathing. Riding animals or vehicles on the beach or between cabins. And bringing in animals, except licensed muzzled dogs.
And in the summer of 1944, a part of Port Said's beach was designated for women and children.
And there was also an article saying the third bathhouses' men bathed from 8 in the morning to 10.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Six: The Most Dangerous Decision [خيال]
b: "I know this decision," said the Black Flag, watching the mirror. "It was written in 49. I was there."
"You have existed since 49?" said Uncle Sobhi.
"I have existed since the first day a flag was hung. But I work once a day. And the rest is sleep."
And Sami, who was standing at the door, said: "What exactly does the black flag mean?"
"It means," said the flag, fixing his tarboosh, "that the sea is not in its mood today. And that you should sit next to your mother."
"And what else is forbidden?"
"Fishing, camels, and sleeping in the cabin at night."
And Sami thought. "And a dog?"
"A dog, if muzzled and licensed, is allowed. And I think this is the most logical decision in the 22 articles."

secs.h: Chapter Seven: A Casino in the Middle of the Sea [حقيقة]
b: And there is something else in the article that seems imaginary, but is real. In 1931, the Suez Canal Company built a casino inside the sea on the Port Fouad beach. And it also built another casino in Port Said, inside the sea water, in the place of the current fishing port. And they were leased to Monsieur Sionini, and they had a theater and a restaurant and an open air cinema.
So one day, Port Said had a building where people stayed up over the sea water, and watched a film under the stars.
We did not find another source to confirm these details, so the article is our only source.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)
And that night, after the people left, Uncle Sobhi closed the cabin, and Sami was still with him, sitting on the sand. And the Black Flag came out of the cabin, and rode on Sami's shoulder.
"I want to show you something," he said.

And with his small hand, he drew a rectangle in the air. And in the rectangle appeared a big casino over the water, with yellow lights, people in suits and dresses, and soft music. And a big screen in the air, showing a silent film.
"That is the casino," whispered Sami.
"The one that was here," said the flag. "Before this beach. And before this Corniche."
And they were quiet as they watched. And after a few minutes, the picture evaporated. And the sea kept moving in the dark, calm and not angry.
"What is this?" said Sami in a low voice.
"This is what remains when people love a place. Even if the building is gone, the feeling stays."

And in reality, the Corniche is now in a development phase. Al-Ahram newspaper published in February 2026 that the Port Said governorate began the biggest project to develop its waterfront, after more than 20 years of stagnation. And it announced that the first phase covers a full kilometer from the restaurant complex to the floating boat.
And in April 2025, Cairo24 website quoted the governor saying the project will not demolish the Corniche entirely, and that parts of the old marble were rehabilitated.
So if you go now, you may find working parts and parts under development. And this is something that changes, so be careful when you come.
(Sources 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)
And in the morning, Uncle Sobhi woke, opened the cabin, and found the small man asleep on the nail. He laughed, and said: "I won't wake you. You still have time."
And Sami came a little later with his mother. "Uncle Sobhi, is the sea nice today?"
And Uncle Sobhi smiled. "You are the one who learned to ask."
"I know it is nice," said Sami. "But I want to hear someone say it."
"Very nice," said Uncle Sobhi. "And in cabin seven someone is sitting, don't be startled. That is our friend."
The riddle: I am smaller than a house, and bigger than a wardrobe. People change in me before they enter the water. And in 1949, 22 articles were written about me. Who am I?
The choices in the game:
1. The beach cabin
2. The lighthouse
3. The ferry
The answer: the beach cabin. In 1949 the municipal council issued a 22 article decision regulating bathing, including a ban on sleeping in the cabins.

[حقيقة] The Sada Al-Balad article says Port Said had no beaches until the early twentieth century because of sand. In 1911 the municipal council began leasing land for wooden bathhouses at 3 and a half pounds. In 1931 two casinos in the sea. In 1944 a section for women and children. In 1949 a 22 article decision. And now a big Corniche development project since 2025.
[خيال] Uncle Sobhi, Sami and the little Black Flag: our own invention.
Your reward: the "Black Flag" card (Rare, No. 015).

16.t: Port Fouad: The Mango Tree That Keeps Secrets
16.p: Port Fouad, Villa and Garden Streets · Port Said
16.tz: In Port Fouad there is a mango tree that saw everything. And never told.

secs.h: Chapter One: A City Planned With a Ruler [حقيقة]
b: When you step off the ferry in Port Fouad, you feel you have entered another city. Its streets are wide and green, its buildings are low, and the houses stand in gardens. The reason is that this city was planned from the start this way.

Ahl Masr newspaper tells that after the First World War, the Suez Canal Company's management decided to build a new city on the eastern, Asian bank, opposite Port Said, to house its workers and employees. Construction began around 1920, on an area of 682 feddans, and the start was about 300 dwellings.
And before that there was nothing in the place except the quarantine building built in 1901. The official opening was on December 21, 1926, and the city was named after King Fouad.
(Source 1 and Source 2 at the end of the file.)

The city was planned on the "garden city" pattern. That means a grid of squares, cut through by lines at 45 degrees, according to the rules taught at the School of Fine Arts in Paris. The streets are wide and planted with trees, and there is a park.

And it has two districts. The first is for workers and employees: semi-attached housing, two floors, each house with a small garden. And the trees planted in them have grown now, and most are mango trees, according to Ahl Masr. And the houses on the corners were for supervisors, so they could watch the workers easily.

And the other district has villas for senior staff, captains, engineers and administrators. Each villa has a different design, and wide gardens separate them. And according to the article, you can recognize them by the big wooden screens that shade the upper floor balcony.
And in another article on the Egy Press website, the small villas in Port Fouad are about 100 years old and were built by the French for canal workers.
(Sources 1, 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: Adam and the First Time [خيال]
b: Back to the story. There is a boy named Adam, eight years old, living in Port Said, who had never crossed the canal. One day, his father said: "Today we will take you to Port Fouad."
"Asia?" asked Adam.
"Asia," said his father laughing.

And they rode the ferry. And Adam held the rail with both hands, looking at the water, telling himself: "I am about to cross to another continent." And when the ferry stopped, he got off onto the quay and looked at his feet, and said to his father: "Do I have to step carefully?"
"Why?"
"Because it's Asia."
His father laughed. "Step however you like."

secs.h: Chapter Four: The Street That Doesn't Look Like Port Said [خيال]
b: They walked in wide streets. Adam looked right and left. Low houses, gardens, trees, and no crowds. "This is not like ours," he said.
"Ours is a city built without much planning," said his father. "And here it was planned with a ruler."
"What does that mean?"
"It means they saw empty land, and sat down to draw."
And Adam loved drawing. He looked around admiringly, and said: "I want to draw something like this."
And at that moment, a small mango fell at his feet, not yet ripe. He looked up, and found a big tree hanging over, covering half the street.
"I am sorry," said the tree in a low voice, like the sound of leaves when the wind moves them. "That fruit came early."
Adam sat on the ground. "Do you talk?"
"I talk when someone listens. It has been a long time since anyone listened."
"You are very old."
"I am one of the first trees here," said the tree. "From the days the land was empty. I was planted here with a small house, and I am still standing beside it."
"What have you seen?"

"I saw workers coming in, and their mothers hanging bread on the laundry line. And I saw children playing. And I saw young men walking for the last time before they traveled. And I saw people grow, and people change, and people move."
"And you stay silent?"
"I keep secrets." And she smiled with her leaves. "That is my job. When someone does something under my shade, I keep it."
"Can you tell me a secret?" said Adam.
"I don't tell people's secrets. They are not my secrets."
"What about your own?"
The tree was quiet for a bit. "I was alone, long ago. A very long time. There were years the street was empty, and I only heard the echo of footsteps."
"That is a sad secret."
"Not very sad," she said. "Because later people came. And everyone who came put something beside me. One put a chair, one put a dove nesting, and one put a child playing beneath me."
"And me?"
"You have just come. You put something."
And Adam thought. And finally, he opened his bag and pulled out a pencil and paper. And drew a small drawing of the tree, with all her leaves. And put it on the ground, under the trunk.
"This is my secret," he said.
"That is the loveliest secret I heard today," said the tree.

And let me tell you something from reality. The trees in Port Fouad are not fiction. Ahl Masr newspaper says every dwelling has a small garden, and the trees planted in them matured and aged, most of them mango. So if you go to Port Fouad and look at the big trees, you may find things that tell.
And the sources also say the city has a French character, and that the streets were planned in the European way. And that the villas have wood and gardens and different designs.
But the tree that talks, and Adam, and the secrets of paper: fiction. And we will not say a particular tree is that one.
(Sources 1 and 3 at the end of the file.)

Adam sat under the tree for a full hour. And his father was in the street talking to an old man, and did not notice. And Adam heard from the tree stories about winter, and storms, and a night a strong wind blew, and the tree held onto her roots telling herself: "I will not move."
"And you did not move," said Adam.
"No. But I was afraid."
"You were afraid?"
"Everyone who loves a place fears for it."
And when the sun began to lean, Adam got up. "I have to go."
"Will you come again?"
"Of course."
"Then take this," said the tree. And a small mango dropped from her, falling into his hand. "When it ripens, it will be sweet. And remember it is from Asia."
On the ferry going back, Adam held the mango, looking at the shore moving away. And his father asked him: "Did you like Port Fouad?"
"A lot."
"What is the best thing?"
Adam thought. "That the trees there listen."
His father smiled, without understanding. And Adam did not explain. He knows there are secrets that should not be told, even if they are the secrets of trees.
And a week later, the mango ripened. And Adam ate it with his mother. And it was sweet. And he felt, while eating, something strange in the taste, like an old warmth, like something bigger than him.

secs.h: Chapter Ten: The Port Fouad Riddle
b: The riddle: I was planned with a ruler and 45 degree angles. Next to me is a bigger city, and between us are 10 minutes of water. Named after a king, and in my streets are mango trees. Who am I?
The choices in the game:
1. Port Fouad
2. Ismailia
3. West Port Said
The answer: Port Fouad. It officially opened on December 21, 1926 under the name of King Fouad.

[حقيقة] Port Fouad was built after the First World War by the Suez Canal Company to house workers and employees, on 682 feddans in the garden city pattern. Construction began around 1920 with about 300 dwellings, and the official opening was December 21, 1926. It has a district for workers and employees and a villa district for senior staff, and many mango trees.
[خيال] Adam and the tree that keeps secrets: our own invention.
