17.t: The French Post Office: The Letter That Never Arrived
17.p: Site of the French Post Office Building, Safia Zaghloul Street (formerly Eugenie) and Memphis Street, Europeans' Quarter · Port Said
17.tz: A letter written long ago in the French Post Office has still not arrived. Who will it reach?

secs.h: Chapter One: A Post Office Before the Canal [حقيقة]
b: In the Europeans' quarter, at the intersection of Safia Zaghloul (formerly Eugenie) and Memphis streets, near Customs Gate number 8, there was a building called the "French Post Office".

The sources say it was built in 1867, so about two years before the opening of the Suez Canal. And it was built by a Frenchman named Jean Baptiste Pierre. It housed a French post office that operated in Port Said from 1867 to 1899, and issued French stamps.

The reason is that Port Said is at the canal entrance, with foreign communities working on the digging, and sailors arriving with ships. And there had to be a post office near the port, a link between these strangers and their faraway families.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Two: The Canal Opening Party [حقيقة]
b: And in the book of the Greek historian Demetrios Galadibis "Memories and Events in Port Said", page 129 according to the source, when the Suez Canal opened a big party was held in the French Post Office building. And the building remained a post office and the residence of the post master, Antoine Grima.

And afterward, according to Dar Al-Mahfouzat documents relayed by Dr. Ahmed Ragab, the building was sold in 1943, on October 9, to a French woman named Therese Joseph Romano, and turned into a nightclub.
And then its ownership moved to a businessman, and it became closed, with cracks and neglect, according to the Basaraha website.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: What Happened in June [حقيقة]
b: And in June 2026, something happened. The Ahl Masr site published that wide anger spread among locals and heritage lovers in Port Said, after news and photos circulated of the demolition of the French Post Office building. And some people on social media said it was the oldest standing building in the city.

And the Basaraha site published the same day that the building was demolished completely as part of development work. We found both, but we found no official statement from the governorate explaining the reason or what will be done on the site.
And also a point: the claim that it is "the oldest building in Port Said" comes from social media posts, not from a study. So we say "one of the oldest buildings" only.
(Source 1 and Source 2 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Four: The Postman Who Did Not Leave [خيال]
b: Back to the story. There was a postman named Anton. Not Antoine Grima whom we mentioned in the sources, this is another name, entirely made up. Anton distributed the letters from the post office to the houses of the Europeans' quarter, with the wooden balconies.
And he had a strange habit: every letter not delivered to its owner, he kept in a small drawer under the window, and wrote on its back: "Not yet".
And years passed. And Anton grew old, and left, and the post office remained. And the drawer remained, and the letters that never arrived remained inside it.

And one day, about a hundred years later, a girl named Lina came, ten years old, with her grandmother. The grandmother was walking in the street telling: "Here there was a post office. And in my childhood, I used to come here with my father on Fridays."
And Lina saw the building. It was standing, with wooden windows, and balconies from which things hung down. And it was locked with chains.
"Grandmother, why is this closed?"
"For years," said the grandmother.
"Can I go in?"
"No, my dear. It is dangerous."
But Lina, with her grandmother busy telling a woman she met, walked toward the door. And she heard a sound from inside, like paper turning. And she looked through a small opening.
There was a man standing, in an old uniform and cap, arranging letters in a big wooden drawer. He saw her, and smiled.
"Welcome, miss. You are late."
"Me?" said Lina, not exactly afraid. "It is my first time here."
"No, miss. There is a letter for you."
"For me?"
"From long ago. From before you were born."

And he pulled a yellow letter from the drawer. On it was written in slanted handwriting: "To whoever will come". "I did not know your name. So I wrote this. Every letter must arrive. Even if it takes a hundred years."
And he held out the letter through the opening in the door, and she took it from his hand.
Lina opened the letter, and there was a single sheet. On it, in compressed letters, was written:

"Dear arrival. If you are reading this letter, then the building still has something to tell. Do not forget that every place has a memory. And that the people who passed here were writing to their families, and waiting for a reply, and worrying. So write to someone you love. Every day."
"Is that all?" said Lina.
"That is a lot," said Anton. "People forget to write."
And Lina kept looking at the paper. And then she pulled a notebook and pen from her bag, and wrote: "Dear Dad, today I went to visit an old place."
And Anton said: "I have a request."
"What?"
"I must go. This building is finished. I won't stay here."
"Where are you going?"
"The letters not yet delivered, I will take them with me. And I will distribute them everywhere. They need not stay here."
And he opened the drawer, and many letters came out of it, flying in the air like small white birds. And went in all directions: toward the canal, toward the street, toward the sea.
And Lina stood watching, tears in her eyes, and in her hand her small letter.
"Will you come again?" she asked.
"Not me," said Anton. "But you. And try to look at places before they disappear."

And let me tell you plainly. The painful truth is that in Port Said buildings go. And the locals themselves said this has been happening in recent months, according to Ahl Masr. And the Port Said governorate has its opinion and point of view on development. But every time an old building goes, the city loses a piece of its memory.
And this is the idea the story was built on. We are not saying what happened was wrong or right. We are saying the story stays, even if the building does not exist.
And Anton and Lina and her grandmother and the yellow letter: fiction. Everything other than that is from the sources.
(Sources 1 and 2 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Ten: The Post Office Riddle
b: The riddle: I was built two years before the canal. The canal's opening party was held at my place. I sent letters for people far from their families. And in the end, I became a story. Who am I?
The choices in the game:
1. The French Post Office
2. The Canal Authority building
3. The train station
The answer: the French Post Office. It was built in 1867, and had a French post office until 1899.

[حقيقة] The French Post Office building was built in 1867 at the intersection of Safia Zaghloul and Memphis streets, and it housed a French post office from 1867 to 1899. Galadibis mentions that the canal opening party was held in it. In 1943 it was sold and turned into a nightclub. Afterward it became closed. In June 2026 reports say it was demolished, and there is anger among locals. We found no official statement.
[خيال] Anton, Lina and the yellow letter: our own invention.
Your reward: the "Letter to Whoever Will Come" card (Rare, No. 017).

18.t: The National Museum: The Statue Tired of Visitors
18.p: Port Said National Museum, Palestine Street opposite the De Lesseps Promenade · Port Said
18.tz: A statue tired of the visitors who ask the same question. Today she has a question of her own.

secs.h: Chapter One: A Museum at the Meeting Point [حقيقة]
b: On Palestine Street, formerly called Sultan Hussein Street, opposite the De Lesseps Promenade, there is a museum called the Port Said National Museum. Its location is special: it is at the point where the waters of the Suez Canal meet the Mediterranean, opposite Customs Gate number 1.

And according to an article on the "Asl Al-Makan" website, the museum holds about 9,000 artifacts from different eras: Pharaonic, Greco-Roman, Coptic and Islamic, up to the modern era. The article describes it as "the first museum of its kind in Egypt", and this is marketing language from the site itself, so we do not confirm it.
And one site says the museum was founded to commemorate the 1956 Battle of Port Said.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Two: It Passed Through Hard Days [حقيقة]
b: According to the same article, work on the museum began in 1963 on an area of 13 thousand square meters, and it opened on Port Said's National Day, December 23, 1964. After that, the article says work on it stopped for about 13 years, from 1967 to 1980, because it was hit by two missiles in the June 1967 war. It was rebuilt and reopened in December 1986, with about 9 thousand pieces spread over 3 halls, and a hall was added displaying the military history of Port Said.
And after that, the article says the museum was developed to be a tourist destination, with a third of the area given to the museum and two thirds to bazaars and shops.

And when we say these years come from one article, this is not an objection to them, it is only so you know that if someone helps us confirm them, it will be better. And in 2012 the Minister of Antiquities announced that the Port Said National Museum project would cost 101 million pounds to build, according to Abu Al-Hol magazine.
(Sources 1 and 2 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: The Statue That Doesn't Like Questions [خيال]
b: Back to the story. Inside the museum, in a small hall on the first floor, there is a small stone statue, called in the story "Sit Al-Kol". She looks like a seated woman, hands on her knees, eyes half closed.
And Sit Al-Kol was tired. Because every day, thousands of people come in front of her, and say the same sentence: "I wonder how old this is?"
And she always wanted to answer: "Very old. Older than you and your grandfather."
But she did not speak. Except when the museum closed and was empty.
And one night, the museum closed, and the lights went off, except a small lamp in the corridor. And there was a new guard named Sayed, on his first day of work. A kind man, who looked a bit scared.
Sayed was walking slowly in the corridor, with a flashlight, telling himself: "Nothing. Just statues. Nothing."
And he heard a voice from the hall: "Are you new?"
Sayed raised the flashlight. And found no one.
"I am here," said the voice. "The seated woman."
And Sayed stopped where he stood. And pressed the flashlight, and pointed it at the statue. And saw her eyes fully open.
"Are you talking?" whispered Sayed.
"At night only," said Sit Al-Kol. "In the day I am busy. I listen to the questions."
"What are the questions?"
"The best: 'Is it real?' and the worst: 'Can I take a photo with the statue?' and the sweetest: 'Mama, is this a lady?'"
Sayed laughed without noticing. "And what do you answer?"
"Nothing. I am a statue." And she sighed. "But at night, if someone asks me, I answer."
"Then I will ask you." Sayed sat on the floor. "How old are you?"
And she looked at him. "I am tired of that question."
"Sorry!"
"No, no," she said. "Fine, I will answer you. I am very old. But I am not the oldest thing here."
"Who is the oldest?" asked Sayed.
"Come."
And Sayed got up and followed her down the corridor to another hall. And in it was a small cracked clay jar, sitting in a corner.
"This?"
"This one saw more people than me. She has worked in the museum since before the museum was built."
"How?"
"She was moved from place to place. From house to house. From soil to soil. And finally she arrived here. And every place she was moved to, she left something in it."
"What?"
"A smell. A memory. A crumb of dust. And when you come close to her, you will smell the smell of all those places."
And Sayed came close, and indeed smelled a strange smell, like soil after rain.

secs.h: Chapter Seven: What Happened at the Museum [حقيقة]
b: And let me tell you something from reality. According to the Asl Al-Makan article, the museum went through a hard period in 1967, when it was hit by two missiles, and was then rebuilt. And this is according to one source. And if it is true, then this building has scars.

And in the story, we stayed away from the scars, because we do not want to invent a story about something that happened in a war. What we tell about the jar and the statue is just fiction, but about the museum itself it is that it saw hard days, and then came back.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

Sayed sat with Sit Al-Kol until dawn. And she told him about all the statues, one by one. And about the jar that likes to snore at night, and the candlestick that changes place every week. And Sayed laughed, and said: "Is this the museum?"
"This is the museum," she said. "Visitors see a quarter of it. Whoever stays at night sees the rest."
And before morning came, she said: "I want something from you."
"Say it."
"If a child comes tomorrow and asks: 'How old is this?' tell him something other than the usual answer."
"What do I tell him?"
"Tell him: 'It doesn't matter. What matters is she is still listening.'"
And in the day, a child named Yasser came, six years old, with his school. He stood in front of Sit Al-Kol, and looked at her closely, and then asked the teacher in a loud voice: "How old is this?"
And the teacher began: "This is from..."
"Wait," said Sayed, who was standing in the corner. "Can I answer?"
And he came close to Yasser, and bent down, and said quietly: "It doesn't matter. What matters is she is still listening."
And Yasser looked at the statue again, and then whispered to Sayed: "Is she listening to me now?"
"Of course."
"Then I want to tell her something." And Yasser came close to the statue, and said in a low voice: "Thank you for still being here."
And in the dim light, Sayed saw, and he was sure, that Sit Al-Kol's eyes shone for a moment.
The riddle: I am opposite a promenade that looks out on the canal, and between two: a sea and a canal. Inside me are things older than the whole city. Who am I?
The choices in the game:
1. Port Said National Museum
2. The Military Museum
3. The Victory Museum
The answer: Port Said National Museum, on Palestine Street opposite the De Lesseps Promenade.

[حقيقة] The museum is on Palestine Street opposite the De Lesseps Promenade, where the canal meets the sea. According to one article: it began in 1963 and opened December 23, 1964, stopped for 13 years after 1967 and was reopened in December 1986, with about 9 thousand pieces in 3 halls. These dates need confirmation.
[خيال] Sit Al-Kol, the guard Sayed, the jar and Yasser: our own invention.
Your reward: the "Sit Al-Kol" card (Rare, No. 018).

3. Watanint, Port Said museums, pages of history (July 15, 2023): https://www.wataninet.com/2023/07/%d9%85%d8%aa%d8%a7%d8%ad%d9%81-%d8%a8%d9%88%d8%b1%d8%b3%d8%b9%d9%8a%d8%af-%d8%b5%d9%81%d8%ad%d8%a7%d8%aa-%d9%85%d9%86-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%aa%d8%a7%d8%b1%d9%8a%d8%ae/

19.t: The Abbasi Mosque: One of One Hundred and Two
19.p: Al-Abbasi Mosque, Al-Arab District · Port Said
19.tz: One of one hundred and two. What makes a single mosque worth a story?

b: In the Al-Arab district of Port Said, there is a mosque called the Abbasi Mosque. It was built in 1322 AH, which is 1904 AD, in the reign of Khedive Abbas Hilmi II. And that is why it is called "Abbasi".

And it was the second mosque in Port Said, after the Tawfiqi Mosque, which is the oldest mosque in the city. And the reason, according to Wikipedia and Al-Watan newspaper, is that Port Said's population was growing fast, and a new mosque was needed to hold the worshippers.

And Cairo 24 newspaper says the Khedive allocated 4,000 meters for the building, and the Awqaf engineers built the mosque on only a tenth of the area. And it opened in 1905 in the presence of the Awqaf director, the Canal governor Mohamed Mohib Pasha, and the judge of Port Said.
(Sources 1, 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)

And there is something special about this mosque. Wikipedia says Khedive Abbas built 102 mosques of the same style in different governorates. So the Abbasi Mosque in Port Said is one of 102 mosques of the same spirit.

And after 100 years from its construction, it was registered as an Islamic monument. And the Awqaf renovated it more than once, and the last renovation, according to Wikipedia, was in 2000. And Al-Watan published in 2018 that Friday prayer was held in it after restoration work.
And we found no reliable source naming the other 101 mosques, so we will not name any of them.
(Sources 1, 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: Magdy and the Matter of Curiosity [خيال]
b: Back to the story. There was a man named Magdy, who worked as a builder. Every day he passed by the Abbasi Mosque on his way to work. And every day he looked at the minaret and the facade, and told himself: "That is nice building."
And one day, he stopped in front of it for a while. And heard, from behind him, the voice of a little girl saying: "Uncle, what are you looking at?"
He turned and found a girl named Nadine, seven years old, holding a school bag bigger than her. "I am looking at the construction," he said.
"Why?"
"Because I am a builder."
"Is it good?"
"Very good."
"Who built it?"
And Magdy went quiet. He did not know.

secs.h: Chapter Four: The Question That Was Not Answered [خيال]
b: "I don't know," he said honestly. "But I will ask."
"I will ask too," said Nadine.
And in the evening, Magdy asked someone from the Awqaf who was passing, who answered him: "This was built in the days of Khedive Abbas Hilmi. It was built on a tenth of the land."
"So the rest stayed empty?"
"I don't know."
And Magdy went home preoccupied with this idea. Imagine: 4,000 meters, and built on only 400. So the rest stayed open space. A garden? A square? A place for children to play?
And he slept dreaming of the land that was left.
In the dream, he was standing in a wide land. And the Abbasi Mosque was in the middle, and around it a big square, and on its edges 101 other mosques, each looking at the other.
And he heard a voice, not with the ear, with the heart: "You came."
"Who are you?"
"We are the siblings. 102 of us. From all the governorates."
"And you talk?"
"We talk without words. Each of us feels the other. When someone builds something on one, the others feel it."
Magdy smiled. "And I am a builder."
"We know," said the voice. "That is why we asked you to come."
"We want to ask you something," said the voice. "Something simple."
"Say it."
"We do not need restoration. The Awqaf does that. Our wish is something else: that someone looks at us."
"Looks?"
"Yes. There are people who pass in front of us every day without looking. And you are the first who looked."
And the voice went quiet, and then said: "And a little girl asked."
"Nadine."
"Nadine. And she will ask a lot. Answer her."
And Magdy woke. It was five in the morning. And he sat on the bed a while, and then dressed, and went to the mosque before work.

And let me tell you a small thing from reality. The Abbasi style is not just a story. According to Wikipedia, Khedive Abbas built 102 mosques in this style. And in Port Said, the mosque is one of the few registered as an Islamic monument.
And also according to Cairo 24, the mosque was built on a tenth of the area allocated. This is a small detail, but it makes you think about the space around it.
But the dream and the siblings and the voice: fiction. And Magdy and Nadine: fiction.
(Sources 1 and 3 at the end of the file.)
And in the morning, while he stood in front of the mosque, Nadine came, with her big bag. And said: "You are still here?"
"Yes. I was waiting for you."
"Why?"
"Because I found out. This mosque was built in 1904. And it has 101 siblings."
"Siblings!" said Nadine excitedly. "That is nice."
"And I came to tell you that you asked a good question."
And Nadine thought, and then said: "Then I will ask again."
"Ask."
"How many bricks does this mosque have?"
And Magdy laughed from his heart. "That is a question nobody knows the answer to."
"Then I will count them."

And from that day, Nadine started counting. Every day on her way to school, she would stand in front of the mosque for a minute, and count the bricks of one row. And after a month, she reached a hundred rows.
"At this rate you will finish in a year," said Magdy, passing by.
"No. I did the math. I will finish in three years."
"And then?"
"And then I will start from the beginning," she said. "Because bricks change."
And Magdy understood that the story is not about counting. It is about looking. And Nadine, without meaning to, was carrying out the mosque's request: that someone look at it every day.
The riddle: I am the second mosque in the city. My name comes from a khedive's name. And I am one of one hundred and two of the same style. Who am I?
The choices in the game:
1. The Abbasi Mosque
2. Al-Salam Mosque
3. The Tawfiqi Mosque
The answer: the Abbasi Mosque. It was built in 1904 in the reign of Abbas Hilmi II, and it is the second mosque in Port Said.

[حقيقة] The Abbasi Mosque in Al-Arab district was built in 1322 AH (1904) in the reign of Khedive Abbas Hilmi II, and opened in 1905 according to Cairo 24. The second mosque in Port Said after the Tawfiqi. Wikipedia says the Khedive built 102 mosques of the same style. It was registered as a monument after 100 years. Last renovation 2000.
[خيال] Magdy, Nadine and the dream of the siblings: our own invention.

20.t: The Tawfiqi Mosque: The Granary That Had a Minaret on Top
20.p: Al-Tawfiqi Mosque, Al-Arab District · Port Said
20.tz: An old granary that had a minaret on top. What changed between then and now?

secs.h: Chapter One: A Mosque in a Granary [حقيقة]
b: When the Suez Canal Company brought Egyptian workers to dig the canal, it built them a mosque in Al-Arab village in 1860. And this mosque was originally a grain depot, meaning a wheat store, with a minaret on it. This is according to Sada Al-Balad and Wikipedia.

And its services were not enough for the growing number of worshippers. And after about 8 years, in 1868, the city administration decided to attend to it. And in June 1869, instructions were issued to rebuild it from wood, but the wood did not last long because of sewage water.
(Sources 1 and 2 at the end of the file.)

And as the city expanded and its population grew, Khedive Tawfiq visited Port Said in 1881. He saw the village mosque, and ordered the Awqaf Authority to rebuild it at its current location, with an attached school for raising children.

And a celebration was held on December 7, 1882, with a huge procession that went around Port Said, led by the scholars, headed by Sheikh Abdel Rahman Abu Al-Hassan, sheikh of the Muslim scholars in Port Said, the judge and the city notables and the heads of the Sufi orders, with music in front of them.
And from here it was named "Tawfiqi" after the Khedive, and became the oldest mosque in Port Said, in Al-Arab district, the heart of the city's oldest quarter.
(Sources 1, 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: Hamza and the Grain of Wheat [خيال]
b: Back to the story. There is a boy named Hamza, nine years old, who likes to walk in the old alleys after school. And in Al-Arab district, he found a narrow alley, with remains of old stone on the ground.
He stopped in front of it, and found beside him a small golden grain of wheat, lying on the ground. A strange thing, because there is no field or farm nearby.
He picked it up in his hand, and it asked him in a voice softer than an ant's: "Do you know where I came from?"
"From a land?" said Hamza.
"From a granary."
"The granary that had a lot of wheat," said the grain. "I am one of them. We came from the Delta, in boats, and unloaded here. And in a big store, and above it a minaret."
"A minaret above a granary?"
"Yes, a strange job." And she gave a small laugh. "We would sleep hearing the call to prayer from above, not understanding what it was, because we are wheat."
And Hamza asked: "And what happened?"
"The store became a mosque. And the wheat was moved. And I stayed. Forgotten in a corner."
"And you were stuck a hundred and fifty years?"
"Not exactly." And she sighed. "I am not an ordinary grain. I am a grain that waits."

secs.h: Chapter Five: What She Waits For [خيال]
b: "What are you waiting for?" asked Hamza.
"Someone to listen to me," said the grain. "All the people who passed here were in a hurry. And you are the first who stopped."
"Me?"
"You look at the ground, and you like the old. And that is exactly what I was waiting for."
And Hamza sat on an old stone, and put the grain on his palm. "So what do you want?"
"I want you to take me to the mosque."
"Why?"
"To see it. I have not seen it since I was moved. But I heard it being built, from far away."
And Hamza got up, and put the grain in his shirt pocket, and walked.
They reached in front of the mosque. It was afternoon, the street was quiet, and the minaret was visible. And Hamza stood on the sidewalk, and took the grain from his pocket, and raised it high.
"Do you see?"
The grain was silent. She said nothing. And then in a changed voice: "I remember this call to prayer."
"It is not the same one."
"Yes, but the place is the same." And she kept looking. "There was a minaret above the granary. And it became a minaret above a mosque. And in both cases, there was a voice coming from above."
And Hamza thought. "So the place kept telling even when it changed?"
"That is the only thing that stays."

secs.h: Chapter Seven: The Truth Steps In [حقيقة]
b: And let me tell you something from reality. The Tawfiqi Mosque is described as the first mosque in the modern city. And Wikipedia says the mosque the Company built for the workers was a "grain depot" with a minaret on it. So the granary story is real.
But the grain, and Hamza, and the dialogue: fiction. And nobody knows whether the wheat that was in the granary is real or not, because the source says only "grain depot".
And the source also says the wooden mosque did not last because of sewage water, meaning the city was still learning to deal with its soft ground between the sea and the lake.
(Sources 1 and 2 at the end of the file.)
Hamza went back home, carrying the grain in his pocket, and put it in a cup with some water. And he woke in the morning, and found the grain sprouted, with a thin green thread.
"You are sprouting!" he said admiringly.
"I told you," answered the grain, in a slightly weaker voice. "I am a grain that waits. And I waited until I saw."
"And now?"
"Now I am ready to grow."
And Hamza planted her in a small pot on the window. And after a week, she had two leaves. And after a month, a small ear of wheat.

secs.h: Chapter Nine: The Ear of Wheat [خيال]
b: And one day, Hamza took the ear, and went to the old alley again. And put it on the ground, beside the stone where he found the grain.
"Why?" asked his friend who was with him.
"Because there are others waiting," said Hamza. "And I can't hear them all. But each one leaves something. And then someone comes to listen."
And his friend laughed. "You are strange."
"Yes," said Hamza, looking at the minaret from far. "And this place is strange too."
The riddle: I was a wheat store with a minaret on top of me. Then I became a mosque. My name comes from a khedive's name. And I am the oldest mosque in the city. Who am I?
The choices in the game:
1. The Tawfiqi Mosque
2. The Abbasi Mosque
3. Al-Salam Mosque
The answer: the Tawfiqi Mosque. The oldest mosque in Port Said, going back to a grain depot with a minaret in 1860.

[حقيقة] The Tawfiqi Mosque is the oldest mosque in Port Said, in Al-Arab district. In 1860 a mosque for workers that was originally a grain depot with a minaret. 1869 rebuilding from wood that did not last. Khedive Tawfiq's visit in 1881, and the celebration on December 7, 1882.
[خيال] Hamza and the grain that waits: our own invention.

21.t: The Cathedral: The Bell That Speaks Three Languages
21.p: Cathedral of the Virgin Mary and the Archangel Michael (Al-Cathedral), facing the sea · Port Said
21.tz: A bell that speaks three languages facing the sea. What does it say to each one?

secs.h: Chapter One: A Church Looking at the Sea [حقيقة]
b: At the intersection of Salah Salem and 23 July streets, facing the sea, there is a big cathedral in the Roman-Byzantine style. Its current name is the Cathedral of the Virgin Mary and the Archangel Michael, and the people of Port Said call it "Al-Cathedral".

Its first name was "Mary Queen of the World", according to a book by the researcher Otto Meinardus, relayed by the Bab Masr website. It was a Latin Catholic church, and the seat of the Apostolic Vicar of the Suez Canal region. And it was built to serve the Latin Europeans, and Italians were a large share of them.
(Sources 1 and 2 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Two: Who Bought the Land [حقيقة]
b: According to the same report, in 1929 King Fouad I permitted the sale of the land, and it was bought by Bishop Ange-Marie Hiral, whose name is tied to the founding of the cathedral. He was born in France in 1871, and died in Quebec in 1952.

And he saw that the church to be built at the canal entrance must be worthy of the place. And the architect was Jean Hulot, according to the information table in the article. Building permit 1932, foundation stone 1934, and the blessing on January 13, 1937.
And Sada Al-Balad says it opened in 1937 and that its idea came from a decision of the Vatican pope in 1930. And Al-Ahram newspaper says the idea began in 1930 by order of Pope Pius XI.
And later the church became affiliated with the Coptic Orthodox. And the first Orthodox mass in it was on February 15, 1987, according to the same report.
(Sources 1, 2, 3 and 4 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: Laila and the Stairs [خيال]
b: Back to the story. There is a girl named Laila, eight years old, who came with her aunt to visit the cathedral. Her aunt works arranging flowers for occasions. And she was busy adjusting the flowers in the nave.
And Laila walked down a side corridor. And found a small staircase, old stone, going up, with a small open lock on it.
"No one is here," she told herself. And went up.
The staircase was long. And each step she heard a small echo. And she reached the top, a wide place with a heavy rope hanging, and above the rope a big bronze bell.
Laila stood in front of the bell. It was very big, three times bigger than her. And when she brought her hand close, she heard a voice coming from it, like a faraway echo:
"Bonjour."
"What?"
"Buongiorno."
And then: "Good morning."
And Laila opened her eyes wide. "You speak three languages?"
"I am the bell of the Cathedral," said the bell in a deep voice. "I was made in a time when the country had French, Italian and Egyptian people. And each of them said good morning in his language."
"And you learned them?"
"I did not learn. I heard."

"In the old days," said the bell, "people would come out from here in French and Italian, talking to each other in the nave. And then the days changed. The people changed. And now they come out in Arabic. And I still say good morning in three languages."
"Why?"
"So I don't forget." And he was quiet a bit. "This place has seen a great many people. And each of them needed someone to say good morning to them."
"And me?"
"You are the first who came up to me in years."
And Laila smiled, and said: "Bonjour, Buongiorno, good morning."
And she heard the echo of the voice ringing in the dome, until it vanished.

And let me tell you something from reality. The article we relied on says the cathedral was originally built for the Latin Europeans, and that Italians were a large share of them. And it says it is now a Coptic Orthodox church. So this building really saw big transformations.
And the church priest told Al-Dostour newspaper in 2023 that there is a huge old picture painted on the ceiling above the old Catholic altar, and that people come from everywhere to see it.
But the bell that speaks: fiction. We found no source describing a bell in such detail. And Laila and her aunt: fiction.
(Sources 1 and 5 at the end of the file.)
And suddenly, Laila heard her aunt's voice: "Laila! Where are you?!"
"I am up here!"
"How did you get up there?!"
Laila went down quickly, in her hand a white feather, which she found beside the bell. And her aunt saw her: "You are not supposed to go up!"
"Sorry. But up there is something beautiful."
"What?"
Laila thought. And in the end said: "A bell that says good morning."
And her aunt laughed and took her in her arms. "You have a big imagination."
And in the morning, Laila came again. But this time, she stood in the nave, and looked up. And heard a small bell ringing, from far away.
And she heard inside it, or imagined she heard: "Bonjour."
And she smiled.
And her aunt asked her: "What are you looking at?"
"At the bell."
"Did you hear it?"
"Yes."
"What does it say?"
And Laila thought. "It says this place is open to everyone."
And her aunt did not reply. But she held her hand, and they walked together toward the door.
They stood on the quay in front of the cathedral. And the sea in front of them, the ships far away. And they saw a ship entering the canal.
"Where is it going?" asked Laila.
"Passing through," said her aunt. "Like many people passed through here."
"And do they come back?"
"Some of them."
And Laila looked at the ship, and thought of the bell. And said: "I feel the bell is greeting all the ships."
"Maybe," said her aunt.
The riddle: I was built facing the sea. I was born Latin and grew up Coptic. And everyone who entered me spoke a different language. Who am I?
The choices in the game:
1. The Cathedral of the Virgin and the Archangel Michael (Al-Cathedral)
2. Al-Salam Mosque
3. The National Museum
The answer: Al-Cathedral. It was built and blessed in 1937 and was Latin, and became Coptic Orthodox.

[حقيقة] The cathedral is at the intersection of Salah Salem and 23 July, Roman-Byzantine style, architect Jean Hulot, Bishop Ange-Marie Hiral bought the land in 1929. Building permit 1932, foundation stone 1934, blessing January 13, 1937. It was Latin Catholic and became Coptic Orthodox, with the first Orthodox mass on February 15, 1987.
[خيال] Laila and the bell that speaks three languages: our own invention.
Your reward: the "Bell" card (Rare, No. 021).

22.t: Port Said Market: The Mannequin Who Remembers All the Customers
22.p: Al-Arab District Markets: Al-Hamidi, Al-Togari, Al-Talateeni and Mohamed Ali Street · Port Said
22.tz: A mannequin in the market remembers all the customers. If you ask her, she will tell you who came and who left.

secs.h: Chapter One: A Whole City as a Market [حقيقة]
b: For many years, Egyptians came to Port Said from every governorate to buy imported clothes. The Beshkateb website (2023) says the city lived its golden age and its markets flourished after Law No. 24 of 1976, which provided for turning the whole city into a free zone.

And then, in 2002, Law No. 5 was issued, which removed the free zone advantage from Port Said. It provided for reducing import quotas over five years: 10% in the first year, 25% in the second and the same in the third, and 20% in the fourth and the same in the fifth, according to the same article.
And then Law No. 6 of 2013 restored the free market system, but the article says it did not succeed in reviving the commercial market again.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

And the article mentions the three most famous commercial markets in Port Said, in the Al-Arab district: "Al-Talateeni", "Al-Togari" and "Al-Hamidi". And it says these markets were empty at the time the article was written in 2023, and that merchants complain of stagnation and of higher prices and fees.

And in 2015, Al-Watan website published that dozens of Port Said merchants organized a march from Mariam Mosque in Al-Manakh district to the commercial Mohamed Ali Street, to demand the return of the free zone.

And in 2010, Asharq Al-Awsat newspaper wrote about the "Bala" market in Port Said, which thousands of Egyptians visit to buy clothes. We only read the article as an excerpt, we did not read its full text.
(Sources 1, 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)
Back to the story. On one of the commercial streets, there was a small clothes shop, its owner Uncle Hamdy. And in the display window, an old mannequin, called in the story "Madam Nagwa".
Madam Nagwa wore a green dress that had not changed in years, and a small cap on her head. Her eyes were a blue drawing, and her hand half raised, as if greeting the people coming.
And every day, when Uncle Hamdy opened the shop, he would say to her: "Good morning, Madam."
And she never answered. But once, on a rainy day, as he was closing the shop, he heard a small voice say: "That jacket is coming fast."
Uncle Hamdy stopped where he was. He looked at the mannequin. And after long thought, said: "Was it you who spoke?"
"I remember," said Madam Nagwa. "I remember all the customers."
"All?"
"From the days when there were lines at the door. People from Alexandria, from Assiut, from Mansoura, from Zagazig. They come by train and get out of the station and run to the market."
"And they dress you?"
"Everyone looks at the dress and says: 'This is nice, if only it were another color.' And I say to myself: 'It is your color that isn't nice.'"
And Uncle Hamdy laughed, because the mannequin had a sharp tongue.
"Do you remember the best customer?" asked Uncle Hamdy.

"Of course. A small man, in a worn suit, who came on a winter day. He stood in front of me for an hour. And then said: 'This is the dress I will give to my mother.' And after he bought it, he said to me: 'You know? This is the first time I have bought something for someone.'"
And she was quiet a bit. "And I felt I had been of use."
"What does that mean?"
"It means I felt I had become important."
And Uncle Hamdy wiped a small tear with the sleeve of the jacket. "I also worked here 40 years. And I felt the same thing."
And he sat on a chair in front of the window, and kept looking at Madam Nagwa, as she looked at the street.

And let me tell you something from reality, without judging. The articles we read all say that for a period, Port Said was a destination for buying clothes from all over Egypt, and that this period ended or changed. And some say merchants and locals still demand a return, and some explain the reasons with laws and economics.
And we are not economists, and we will not say what is right. What we do is tell about what was: people coming by train, buying, and going back to their families.
And in the story, Uncle Hamdy and Madam Nagwa and the small customer: all fiction, and every real shop that opens or closes today has nothing to do with the story.
(Sources 1, 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)
And on one of the Fridays, the market is full. And Uncle Hamdy opened the shop early, and Madam Nagwa saw everything from the window. And a whole family came: a mother and father and three children.
The little child stood in front of the mannequin, and pointed his finger: "Mama, this one is moving."
"She is not moving, my dear."
"No, she blinked."
And Madam Nagwa really did blink. But very quickly, and nobody noticed except the child.
"Can I take her?" said the child.
"No, my dear," said Uncle Hamdy tenderly. "She is not for sale. She is the shop's companion."
"Can I say hello to her?"
"Say hello."
And the child shook, with his small hand, the mannequin's hand.

secs.h: Chapter Eight: Madam Nagwa Is Moved [خيال]
b: That night, after the shop closed, Madam Nagwa said to Uncle Hamdy: "I want to tell you something."
"Say it."
"I am not sad that the market has calmed. I am only sad that nobody asks me."
"I ask you."
"You are the only one." And she smiled. "But that is enough."
And Uncle Hamdy got up, and put a small shawl on her shoulder. "It will be cold."
"I am a mannequin."
"And you also need warmth."
"Uncle Hamdy," said Madam Nagwa before he slept. "Will this shop stay?"
"I don't know."
"And you?"
"I don't know."
"And if not?"
"We will stay," said Uncle Hamdy after thinking. "Even if not here. We will stay in the memory of those who passed."
And Uncle Hamdy slept. And Madam Nagwa kept looking at the street, with a dim light from a lamp post. And she thought of the small customer, and the dress, and a color that needed to change.
The riddle: People used to come to me by train from every town. I am a city that is all shops. In 1976 I was turned into a free zone. Who am I?
The choices in the game:
1. Port Said
2. Ismailia
3. Damietta
The answer: Port Said. Law 24 of 1976 turned it into a free zone.

[حقيقة] Law 24 of 1976 turned Port Said into a free zone, Law 5 of 2002 removed the advantage and reduced import quotas over five years, and Law 6 of 2013 restored the free market but did not revive the market according to the article. The most famous markets of Al-Arab district: Al-Talateeni, Al-Togari and Al-Hamidi.
[خيال] Uncle Hamdy, Madam Nagwa and the small customer: our own invention.
Your reward: the "Madam Nagwa" card (Common, No. 022).

23.t: The Obelisk: The Flame Waiting for December 23
23.p: Martyrs Square (the Obelisk), 23 July Street, Al-Sharq District · Port Said
23.tz: A flame waiting for December 23 every year. What do you think it is waiting for?

secs.h: Chapter One: A Square Named After an Obelisk [حقيقة]
b: On 23 July Street in Al-Sharq district, in front of the Port Said Governorate headquarters, there is a square named Martyrs Square, and the people of Port Said call it "the Obelisk". The reason for the name is that in the middle of the garden is a monument in the shape of a Pharaonic obelisk covered in gray granite.

According to Wikipedia, this monument was made to commemorate the martyrs of Port Said in its battles. The obelisk was set on a base with a flame on top, and under it the Victory Museum of Modern Art.
And the square's area is about 15 thousand square meters, according to Wikipedia.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

President Gamal Abdel Nasser opened the obelisk and the square on December 23, 1958, on Victory Day, the second anniversary of the withdrawal of the attacking forces from Port Said. And at the ceremony, the Victory flame was lit, according to Wikipedia and the Al-Nabaa website.

And since then, a wreath of flowers has been placed on the monument every December 23 in loyalty to the memory of the martyrs, according to the Tahya Masr website. And in the garden there are statues, including the statue of General Abdel Moneim Riad, according to Al-Nabaa website.
(Sources 1, 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: Uncle Farghaly and the Garden [خيال]
b: Back to the story. In the garden around the obelisk, there was a gardener named Uncle Farghaly. An old man, quiet, who woke at dawn every day, and watered the flowers and trees, and trimmed the grass by hand.
And Uncle Farghaly had a rule: he did not talk while working. He talked only after he finished. And he used to say: "This place doesn't like noise."
And one day, two days before December 23, a girl named Hadeer came, eight years old, with her school, to plant flowers around the monument. And she was holding a paper and pen.
"Uncle, can I ask you?"
"Ask, after I finish."
Hadeer waited next to him until he finished the soil. And then asked: "The flame on top, does it go out?"
"According to the occasion," said Uncle Farghaly. "It is lit on the important days."
"And after that?"
"It waits."
"What does it wait for?"
And the gardener thought. "Next year."
"And does it get tired of waiting?"
And Uncle Farghaly laughed. "I don't know. But I won't get tired."
And Hadeer wrote on her paper: "The flame waits."
And on the night of December 22, the square was quiet. And Uncle Farghaly closed the garden and left. And Hadeer was still holding the paper, and came with her father to buy something nearby.
She stood in front of the obelisk and looked up, and found the flame small, still, lit lightly.
"Do you get tired?" she whispered.
And she heard a warm voice, from above: "No."
"Are you waiting?"
"Yes."
"Why?"
"Because every year people come. And stand here. And the square is quiet. And I love that quiet."
And Hadeer was silent. And then said: "Can I stand here tomorrow?"
"You surely will. And everyone."
"What do you see from up there?" asked Hadeer.
"I see the Governorate building in front of me. And 23 July Street. And people passing in cars. And children running."
"And what do you imagine?"
"I don't imagine. I remember."
"Who?"
"The people I did not see. But I know they were here."
And Hadeer understood that the flame does not tell stories of particular people. She only carries the memory.
And she said: "I will bring you flowers tomorrow."
"I don't need them. But if you bring them, I will be happy."

And let me tell you the part from reality. The monument really has a flame. And really under it is a museum called the Victory Museum of Modern Art. And really a wreath of flowers is placed every December 23. All of this is written in the sources.

But the flame that talks, and Uncle Farghaly, and Hadeer: fiction. And we are not saying the flame is lit at a particular time other than the days the sources mention. We found no source saying it goes out the rest of the year, so that part of the dialogue is entirely fiction.
(Sources 1, 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)
And the day came. The square was full. And Uncle Farghaly was standing in a corner, watching silently. And Hadeer, wearing a wool coat, holding a small bouquet of flowers.
She entered the line, and stood in front of the monument. And put the flowers on the ground gently.
And when she raised her head, she saw the flame shining a little brighter. And she was not sure, but she felt it was smiling.
And she heard inside her: "Thank you."
She did not answer. But she nodded her head, and stayed standing.

secs.h: Chapter Nine: After the People Left [خيال]
b: At night, the square was empty. And Uncle Farghaly came back to close the garden. He found the small bouquet still in its place.
He stood in front of it a while. And then raised his hand gently, and touched the edge of the paper it was tied with. And on it was written in a child's handwriting: "For the flame. From Hadeer."
And he smiled. And went to bring a bucket of water, and watered the bouquet, so it would live longer.
The riddle: I am an obelisk, but not very Pharaonic. Above me is a flame and below me a museum. Flowers are placed at me on the city's holiday. Who am I?
The choices in the game:
1. The Martyrs Obelisk in Martyrs Square
2. The Lighthouse
3. The De Lesseps pedestal
The answer: the Martyrs Obelisk. It opened on December 23, 1958 and has the Victory Museum under it.

[حقيقة] The Martyrs Obelisk is in Martyrs Square, 23 July Street, in front of the Governorate headquarters. Covered in gray granite, with a flame above and the Victory Museum below. It opened December 23, 1958 in the presence of Gamal Abdel Nasser. A wreath of flowers is placed on it every December 23.
[خيال] Uncle Farghaly, Hadeer and the flame that talks: our own invention.
Your reward: the "Flame" card (Rare, No. 023).

24.t: The Victory Museum: The Painting That Kept Looking at the Door
24.p: Victory Museum of Modern Art, under the Martyrs Obelisk, 23 July Street · Port Said
24.tz: A painting in the museum always looked toward the door. Who is it waiting for?

secs.h: Chapter One: A Museum Under an Obelisk [حقيقة]
b: Under the Martyrs Obelisk on 23 July Street, in front of the Governorate headquarters, there is a museum called the Victory Museum of Modern Art. The Fine Arts Sector website says it was made in appreciation of the struggle of Port Said and its people, and to document their heroism.

And Al-Ahram newspaper says it opened on December 25, 1995, within the city's National Day celebrations. And it holds about 75 artworks by great Egyptian artists: sculpture, painting, drawing, graphics and ceramics, most of them on national themes and patriotic events and the subject of war and peace.
(Sources 1 and 2 at the end of the file.)

The Minister of Culture reopened the museum on April 22, 2013 after its development in cooperation with the Port Said Governorate, according to the Maspero website, after a closure of four years, on an area of about 784 square meters.

And in March 2021, the Minister of Culture and the governor of Port Said inspected a new museum display scenario for the museum. And Al-Masry Al-Youm newspaper, in September 2025, described it as having a rare collection of photos, paintings and statues that follow the birth of Port Said, the digging of the canal and the popular resistance.
(Sources 1, 2, 3 and 4 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: Israa and the Assignment [خيال]
b: Back to the story. There is a girl named Israa, ten years old, and at school they gave her an assignment: go to the museum and draw a painting she likes and write about it.
And Israa hated drawing. Not because she did not love it, but because she was afraid that what she drew would not come out as it was in her head.
She entered the museum with her father, and walked from hall to hall. And every painting she looked at, she said to herself: "Nice, but it is not the one."
And in the last hall, she stopped in front of a small painting, with a house and a window and a man looking out of the window.
"This one," she said.
Israa sat on the floor, and opened her notebook, and began drawing. But after a minute, she heard: "You are drawing me wrong."
She stopped. And looked around. Her father was watching another painting, far away. And the voice was coming from the painting.
"You?"
"Yes. The man in the window."
"I am sorry. What is wrong?"
"You are drawing my eyes closed. My eyes are open. I am waiting."
"Waiting for what?"
"The door. For a long time. I have never seen it open."
And Israa looked at the painting closely. In it was a small house, and a wooden door at the end of the picture, far away, almost shaded.
"Is it in the picture?" she asked.
"Yes. But it doesn't open. I have stood here since the day I was painted, waiting for someone to enter."
"Who?"
"The one who painted me did not say."
And Israa thought. "Can I open the door for you?"
"How?"
"I draw it open."
And the man was quiet. And then said in a hesitant voice: "That will not change the original painting."
"No. But it will change my painting."

And let me tell you something. The real museum has 75 works according to the source, but the source does not name these works. So we invented a painting and a man and a window and a door. And nobody needs to look for it in the museum, because it does not exist.

And an important real piece of information: the museum displays works about "war and peace", according to the Fine Arts website. And the idea of an artist looking at something and turning it into a picture is a useful idea for any visitor.
And Israa and the man in the painting: fiction.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)
Israa drew a house and a window and a man. But this time, she drew the door open, and in the door a light, and in the light the face of a woman laughing.
And she heard the man from the original painting say: "Who is this?"
"I don't know. I only drew her."
"Beautiful."
"You can see?"
"I see. From your painting."
"So the door opened?"
"In your painting, yes."
And Israa smiled for the first time since she entered the museum.

secs.h: Chapter Eight: What Happened at School [خيال]
b: The next day, Israa handed the painting in to the school. And the teacher looked at it, and said: "This is nice. Who is in the door?"
"I don't know."
"So you drew her from your imagination?"
"From someone else's imagination," said Israa. "But I am the one who opened the door."
And the teacher did not understand. But hung the painting on the wall.
And one night, while Israa slept, she dreamed of the man. He was standing in front of an open door, and entering. And before he disappeared, he looked at her and said: "Thank you."
A month later, Israa went back to the museum. She walked to the last hall. She stood in front of the painting. The man was still in the window, his eyes open.
"I came back," she said.
"I know."
"Is the door still closed?"
"Yes. But I am not sad. I know there is another place, with an open door."
"In my notebook?"
"In your notebook."
And Israa laughed. "I will bring you more paper."
"I will wait for you."
The riddle: I am under a monument, and above me is a flame. Inside me are 75 artworks. I opened in 1995. Who am I?
The choices in the game:
1. The Victory Museum of Modern Art
2. The Military Museum
3. The Port Said National Museum
The answer: the Victory Museum. It opened December 25, 1995 under the Martyrs Obelisk.

[حقيقة] The Victory Museum of Modern Art is under the Martyrs Obelisk, opened December 25, 1995, and holds about 75 artworks. It was renovated and reopened in 2013 after a four-year closure. In 2021 a new display scenario was inspected.
[خيال] Israa, the painting and the man in the window: our own invention.
Your reward: the "Open Door" card (Common, No. 024).

25.t: The Land That Was Made: The Story of a City Built From Dredge Sand
25.p: The Founding of Port Said and Al-Gamil Village · Port Said
25.tz: A city built from dredge sand. Before it became a city, what was here?

secs.h: Chapter One: A Land That Did Not Exist [حقيقة]
b: On April 25, 1859, De Lesseps began digging the Suez Canal in the reign of Said Pasha. And at the same time work began on building the modern city of Port Said, which at the time was a village called Al-Gamil, about 9 kilometers from the current site of Port Said, so it would be at the northern entrance of the canal.

And one of the first things made in the city was a temporary wooden lighthouse. But there is a problem: the Port Said coast, between the Mediterranean and Lake Manzala, is not high above sea level. So landfill was needed.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

According to Wikipedia, the dredgers that were digging to prepare the coast for docking and make the port basin removed huge quantities from the depths of the water and added them to the lands of Port Said. And the marshes of Lake Manzala were also filled with the sand produced by the dredging, so that housing, warehouses, workshops and a brick factory could be built on them.

And a small canal was dug to connect Port Said's facilities with Lake Manzala, to make it easier to carry supplies and drinking water by boat. And a mosque was built for the workers in Al-Arab village. And two breakwaters were built, west and east, of stone, and after them a new concrete lighthouse that lights up to a distance of 20 miles.
So really: a large part of the city was made from the sand that came out of the digging.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: An Engineer Named Kamal [خيال]
b: Back to the story. Imagine a young engineer named Kamal, made up, working in the workshops in the city's first days. His job is to measure the height of the land after landfill. Every morning he holds a long measuring tool, and goes down with it into the ground, and writes the number.
And every day, the number grows a centimeter. And Kamal would laugh and say: "The land is rising."
And his colleague, a technician named Noaman, would answer: "It is not rising, we are the ones raising it."
"No," Kamal would say. "It is rising. We just help it."

secs.h: Chapter Four: The Night the Land Spoke [خيال]
b: And one night, Kamal stayed alone in the workshop after the people left. And he was calculating numbers. And suddenly he heard a voice coming from under his feet, like the sound of sand moving:
"Are you the one counting me?"
Kamal jumped. "Who?"
"I am the land."
"The land?!"
"The new land. Just born a week ago."
And Kamal sat on the crate. And after a moment, said: "What are you made of?"
"Sand. Clay. Many things that came from under the water." And she gave a rough laugh. "Nobody asks me before building on me."
"I am sorry," said Kamal. "I thought the land is something that already exists."
"I do not exist. I am being made." And in a lighter voice: "But I am not sad. I am proud."
"Why?"
"Because I am the first city built from zero. And then people will come from everywhere, and live on top of me."
And Kamal was silent. And then said: "Can I do something for you?"
"Yes. Promise me something."
"What?"
"When the city grows, do not forget it was built from sand."

And let me tell you something from reality. Al-Gamil is not just an old name. According to Wikipedia, it was a village 9 kilometers from today's Port Said, and it was the point the project started from. And according to an article about Lake Manzala, "Bughaz Al-Gamil" is one of the openings connecting the lake to the Mediterranean.

And in 1956 battles took place in the Al-Gamil area, according to the Military Museum, and a model of the Battle of Al-Gamil is in its yard. But this story is not about the battle, it is about the beginning of the place. So we leave that subject to the museum.
And the land that spoke and Kamal and Noaman: fiction.
(Sources 1, 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)

And in the same period, according to Wikipedia, the new lighthouse was built of concrete, and it lights up to a distance of 20 miles. This is the lighthouse we tell about in story number 1 in the game.
And to know the size of the work: 6 thousand guests were invited to the canal opening ceremony in 1869, according to the same source. This is the ceremony we will tell about in another story.
But the point here is that the city that hosted this ceremony was only ten years old. And it had been built from zero on filled land.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)
Kamal grew up, and became an old man. And one day, walking in Port Said after forty years, he stopped in a square and told himself: "I am standing on sand."
And he smiled. And heard, from under his feet, a voice lighter than before: "Yes."
"You are still here?"
"I am everywhere."
And Kamal sat on the sidewalk, and reached out his hand, and took a handful of soil. And opened it in front of his eyes. "Is this from the days of the dredgers?"
"This is from other days. But I remember."
"I remember too," said Kamal. "I promised you."
"Did you keep it?"
"I told my children. And they told their children. And all of them know Port Said was built from sand."
"That is enough."
And Kamal smiled. And got up, and walked. And in his hand, the handful of soil stayed, until he reached the sea. And he lowered it into the water gently.
The riddle: I did not exist, and I was made from dredge sand. I began as a village 9 kilometers away. Now I am a city. Who am I?
The choices in the game:
1. Port Said
2. Ismailia
3. Suez
The answer: Port Said. It was built from 1859 on land filled with digging output.

[حقيقة] Port Said began April 25, 1859, from Al-Gamil village 9 km from the current site. Its land was filled with the output of dredger digging and the sand and marshes of Manzala. The first lighthouse was temporary wood and after it a concrete lighthouse that lights 20 miles.
[خيال] Kamal, Noaman and the land that talks: our own invention.
Your reward: the "The Land That Was Made" card (Rare, No. 025).

26.t: The Party of Six Thousand: The Banquet Held in a Ten-Year-Old City
26.p: Port Said Port, Canal Entrance, the 1869 Opening · Port Said
26.tz: A huge banquet in a city only ten years old. Who was invited?

secs.h: Chapter One: A Very Big Invitation [حقيقة]
b: According to Wikipedia, Port Said saw huge preparations for the Suez Canal opening ceremony in 1869. Cleanliness was attended to in the places the guests would visit, and care was taken over the uniforms of the soldiers who would receive the invitees. The public streets were cleaned and decorated and lit with lanterns, and flags were hung.

And Khedive Ismail charged De Lesseps with preparing to receive 6 thousand invitees. He brought five hundred cooks and a thousand servants. And he instructed the provincial governors to send local people in their traditional dress, so they spread along the canal: peasants, Upper Egyptians, Bedouins, Sudanese and others.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

And the Egyptian fleet lined up in Port Said port to keep order and add to the joy. And three platforms were made, covered in silk and brocade: the big one for kings, princes and senior invitees, the second on the right for Islamic clergy, and the third on the left for Christian clergy.

And also, according to another source on the same page, a big party was held in the French Post Office building in the Europeans' quarter, according to the historian Demetrios Galadibis, as we told in story number 17.
(Sources 1 and 2 at the end of the file.)
Back to the story. Among the five hundred cooks, there was a cook named Master Sayed Al-Helw. His job was simple: he was in charge of the tea. But not just any tea. The tea of the great guests.
And three days before the party, Master Sayed sat in front of 300 teapots, and said: "Now everything is ready."
And there was a small boy named Mansour, ten years old, helping him. "Master, will these people drink tea or not?"
"They will drink."
"And will they like it?"
"They must like it."
And on the night before the party, Master Sayed discovered a disaster. The sugar was gone.
"The sugar?!" said Mansour. "How?"
"One of the servants took sacks, and went to sell them."
"So what is the solution?"
And Master Sayed thought. "We go to the port. The ships coming in may have some."
"At night?"
"Yes."
And the two went, running along the quay, the lanterns lit everywhere, people preparing the platforms. And they searched around many ships, without luck.
And at the end of the quay, a small boat stood. And an old man sat on the edge, smoking. "Good evening."
"Good evening," said Master Sayed. "Do you have sugar?"
"I do."
"How much?"
"Not for money." The man smiled. "I am going to the party. If you invite me, I will give you all I have."
And Sayed thought. He was not in charge of invitations. "I can't promise you."
"Then take something without a promise." And he pulled out a bag of sugar, and gave it to him.
"Why?"
"Because I was a cook too."

secs.h: Chapter Six: The Night of the Party [خيال]
b: The tea was made, and went to the platforms. And the great guests drank, and all said: "Nice." And Sayed stood in the back, watching, feeling a small pride.
And Mansour came to him and whispered: "Master, the man who owns the sugar is here."
"Where?"
"There. Standing in the last row."
And Sayed looked. And saw an old man, in simple clothes, standing and watching the platforms with shining eyes. And Sayed smiled, and went to him with a cup of tea, and handed it to him.
"This is from Master Sayed," he said. "For the trust."

And let me tell you the real part. The source says preparations were indeed made for 6 thousand invitees, five hundred cooks and a thousand servants, and three platforms. All of this is from Wikipedia, and it relies on a historical reference.
But no source names a particular cook, or a sugar problem, or a boy named Mansour. All of this is fiction. And everything that happened between Sayed and the old man: our own invention.

And an important detail: the source tells about Port Said's preparations and the guests who would pass through it, and does not fix the details of the whole program. So we do not say who did what at what hour.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)
The next day, Master Sayed woke late. And outside, people were taking apart the platforms. And Mansour stood by him: "Master, there are people who want you."
"Who?"
"There are cooks from the ships. They came to greet you."

And Sayed went out, and found twenty cooks, of different nationalities, standing in front of the door. And saying in different languages something he did not understand. And Mansour translated: "They say the tea was nice."
And Sayed laughed. "Tell them the sugar was a gift from a stranger."
And in the afternoon, Sayed found at his kitchen door another bag of sugar. With a small note: "From the friend. If you need."
There was no name. But Sayed knew.
And he went to the small boat, and found it empty. The man had left.
"Where did he go?" asked Mansour.
"I don't know. But he was a cook like us."
And Sayed went to the kitchen, and made a pot of tea, and poured two cups, and sat next to Mansour, and they drank in quiet.
The riddle: They prepared for 6 thousand guests. Five hundred cooks and a thousand servants. Three platforms of silk. The city was only ten years old. Who am I?
The choices in the game:
1. Port Said
2. Alexandria
3. Damietta
The answer: Port Said, the city that prepared for the canal opening in 1869.

[حقيقة] The canal opening in 1869: preparation for 6 thousand invitees, 500 cooks and 1,000 servants, three platforms covered in silk, the Egyptian fleet in the port, and locals in their dress along the canal. According to Wikipedia.
[خيال] Master Sayed, Mansour and the owner of the sugar: our own invention.
Your reward: the "Bag of Sugar" card (Common, No. 026).

27.t: The Quarantine: The Only Building Before the City
27.p: The Quarantine Building and the East Bank, before Port Fouad · Port Said
27.tz: A building alone before the city was built. What was it guarding?

b: Before Port Fouad was built, the east bank of the canal opposite Port Said was barren land. And an article by Hani Abdel Aziz on the Al-Maraya website says that until May 1, 1925 there was no building there except the quarantine building, "the Quarantine", built in 1901, to isolate travelers sick with infectious diseases.
And Ahl Masr and Sada Al-Balad say the same: the only building in the area before the city was the 1901 quarantine building.
(Sources 1, 2 and 3 at the end of the file.)

And the article tells that with the growth of traffic in the canal and ship loads, the Canal Company was forced to build warehouses, workshops and depots on the east bank. And the workers there complained that their working conditions were harder than their colleagues in Port Said, because the east bank was "barren land, deprived of every resource".

So after negotiations with the Egyptian government lasting five years, agreement was reached to use the land east of the canal on May 1, 1925. And the municipal council decided in its session of November 21, 1920 to give it the name "Port Fouad", instead of "East Port Said" which the Company had intended.
And when it officially opened on December 21, 1926, King Fouad arrived in Port Said on the royal yacht "Al-Mahrousa" on the evening of December 20.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Three: The Building That Is Not Welcoming [خيال]
b: Back to the story. Imagine this building, alone in the desert. Watching the ships pass, and the people aboard looking at it. Nobody likes to look at a quarantine building. It is a place for people who are not allowed to enter.
And in the story, the building is named "Uncle Quarn". He is a character who loves people, but he is sad, because nobody visits him by choice.
And Uncle Quarn had a habit: every time a ship passed, he would raise one of his windows, and say: "Thank God for your safety."
And the people on the ship did not hear. But he said it.

One day, a small ship arrived, and a boy named Tawfiq got off it. Eight years old. His father was with him, and they were returning from a long trip, and his father was a bit ill, so they were held in the building for a few days.
Tawfiq was upset. He did not understand why he was held. His father was in bed, and he sat on a chair beside him.
"Dad, why are we here?"
"So people feel reassured."
"And we are not reassuring?"
"We are reassuring. But people must be sure."
And at night, when his father slept, Tawfiq heard a voice from the wall: "Not sleeping?"
And he looked and found the wall quiet. "Who?"
"I am the building."
"You talk?"
"When someone feels lonely, yes."
"I am not alone. My father is beside me."
"I know." And the wall's voice became lighter. "But I am the one who is alone."
And Tawfiq sat on the floor, and held his hand under his head. "Then I will talk with you."
"Nice. Tell me."
And Tawfiq kept telling. About the ship he rode. About the sea. About the people he met. About a far country with red trees.
And Uncle Quarn told him: about the empty land. About the wind. About the day the first ships came. About the emptiness around him, with nothing but him.
"Do you remember anything else?" asked Tawfiq.
"I remember that I was alone. And I stopped being alone when someone sat with me."
And they were quiet a bit. And then Tawfiq said: "I will stay with you."
"Until you leave."
"Yes."
"That is enough."

And let me tell you something from reality. The real building was built in 1901 to isolate travelers sick with infectious diseases, according to the article. And this is exactly the purpose of any quarantine of that time.

And after Port Fouad was built in the twenties, we found no source saying what happened to the building. It may have been demolished, and it may still exist in a different form. So this story does not say it still exists, nor that it disappeared.
And Uncle Quarn and Tawfiq and his father: fiction. And the idea that the building talks: fiction.
(Sources 1 and 2 at the end of the file.)
After five days, Tawfiq's father was well, and they were allowed to leave. As they walked from the door, Tawfiq stopped. And turned, and looked at the building.
And he heard a faint voice: "Goodbye."
And Tawfiq stood on one leg, and said: "I will come back to you."
"Nobody comes back."
"I will come back."
"And if you don't?"
"I will remember you."
And Uncle Quarn was quiet. And then said: "That is enough."
And after about 20 years, buildings began to be built around the building. Young people, workers, and families. And there was the sound of knocking all day.
And Uncle Quarn felt the place changing. From empty land to a city. And from wind to the laughter of children.
"I am not alone," he whispered one day.
And the wind answered: "Not once."
The riddle: I am the only building that was on the east bank. I was built in 1901 to isolate the sick. After me a whole city was built. Who am I?
The choices in the game:
1. The quarantine building (Al-Quarantina)
2. The Lighthouse
3. The train station
The answer: the quarantine building. Built in 1901 and the only one before the city of Port Fouad.

[حقيقة] The quarantine building (Al-Quarantina) was built in 1901 to isolate sick travelers, and was the only one on the east bank before Port Fouad. The agreement with the government on May 1, 1925 and the opening on December 21, 1926. We found no source about the building's fate.

28.t: The De Lesseps Promenade: The Locks That Don't Open
28.p: De Lesseps Tourist Promenade, on the Canal · Port Said
28.tz: Locks hanging on the De Lesseps Promenade, and they don't open. Why?

secs.h: Chapter One: The Corner of the World [حقيقة]
b: The De Lesseps Promenade stretches along the canal in front of the tourist port. The city's people call it "De Lesseps Stone", and also call it "the Corner of the World", because it looks out on two continents: Asia on the Port Fouad side, and Africa on the Port Said side.

It is about 200 meters long, and has two entrances: a northern one, where the base of De Lesseps' statue stood before it was removed, and a southern one toward Egypt Square. And it is designed to be a safe place for families to stroll, away from the crowd of cars and motorbikes. All of this is according to the Sawt Al-Qabaail Al-Arabiya website.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Two: The Statue and the Base [حقيقة]
b: And the statue was erected at the northern entrance of the canal on November 17, 1899, according to the source. This is the date we told about in the story of De Lesseps' pedestal, number 6.

And the Bab Masr website says the features of the promenade began to take shape with the founding of Port Said, and the area at first was a quay and an iron fence separating passersby from the water, and facing it statues and maritime buildings and moorings. With time it became a commercial and social destination, with phone shops, restaurants and ice cream. And then a development project was launched in phases, starting with the tourist port and then the promenade itself.
(Sources 1 and 2 at the end of the file.)
Back to the story. On a summer evening, there was a girl named Yasmin, twenty years old, and a young man named Karim, 22. They were walking on the promenade, on their first outing together.
And Yasmin was nervous. And Karim too. And neither knew how to start talking.
"The sea is nice," said Karim, looking at the canal.
"Yes," said Yasmin.
"And the ships are big."
"Yes."
And they were quiet. And then Yasmin saw on the fence a group of small locks, each with letters on it.

And let me tell you something from reality. According to Sawt Al-Qabaail, lovers keep putting iron locks on the promenade's wires, as an expression of their hope that their love will last. This is a tradition that really exists in many cities of the world, and here it is done too.
And if you go to the promenade, you may find locks. But the number of locks and their size changes with time and development.
(Source 1 at the end of the file.)

secs.h: Chapter Five: The Lock That Was Not Locked [خيال]
b: "Do you have a lock?" asked Yasmin, laughing for the first time.
"No." Karim smiled. "I thought that would be very advanced."
"Me too."
And they were quiet. But the mood became lighter.
And then Yasmin found a small lock, open, thrown on the ground, which nobody had locked. "Come."
And she took it. And it had old letters on it, almost erased. "This is somebody's from long ago."
"Can we write on it?"
"We don't have a key."
"Neither does it." And Karim touched the lock. "It is made so it does not open."
And suddenly, the lock spoke: "I was not locked."
And Yasmin stumbled, and Karim caught her. "What is this?"
"I am a lock. I am talking to you."
"Why were you not locked?"
"Because the one who put me could not lock me. His hand was shaking."
"Why?"
"He was doing something important, and he was afraid."
And Yasmin looked at Karim. And Karim looked at the lock. "Was he apologizing?"
"Apologizing, or asking. I did not understand."
"Will you lock me?" asked the lock.
"I want to," said Yasmin, "but not now."
"Why?"
"Because I am still getting to know him."
And Karim smiled. "I am in no hurry either."
"Fine," said the lock. "I will wait. I am a patient kind of lock."
And Yasmin put it in her pocket. "I will keep you with me until we decide."
And Karim said: "Can we come again?"
"Of course."
They came back after a week, with coffee. And found the promenade quiet, the ships passing. And they sat on the edge, and Karim handed Yasmin the cup.
"Are you nervous?" she asked.
"Less."
"Me too."
And they were quiet a bit, and then Yasmin took out the lock. "Remember?"
"I remember."
"I thought. We won't lock it here."
"Why?"
"Because I want to lock something bigger."
"What?"
"I don't know." And she laughed. "But I will tell you when I know."

secs.h: Chapter Nine: The Lock in the Water [خيال]
b: In the end, Yasmin and Karim went down to the edge of the promenade, and stood. And Yasmin reached out her hand, and opened the lock with her finger, and quietly threw it into the water.
"Why?" asked Karim.
"Because love doesn't have to be locked."
And Karim smiled. "That is nice."
"I took it from the lock."
And they heard, from far away, a small voice saying: "Thank you."
The riddle: I am not a street, and I am not a quay. My length is 200 meters. They call me the corner of the world. On my fence are locks. Who am I?
The choices in the game:
1. The De Lesseps Promenade
2. The Port Said Corniche
3. Port Said Port
The answer: the De Lesseps Promenade. It is about 200 meters long, and looks out on two continents.

[حقيقة] The De Lesseps Promenade is about 200 meters long, on the canal in front of the tourist port, with two entrances. It looks out on Asia and Africa. De Lesseps' statue was erected on November 17, 1899 at its northern entrance. Lovers put locks on the wires.
[خيال] Yasmin, Karim and the lock that talks: our own invention.
Your reward: the "Lock That Wasn't Locked" card (Rare, No. 028).
